"Preliminary investigations found that the Proton Saga carrying the couple was driven by a 20-year-old man, with another passenger, a 21-year-old woman. They were travelling from Cheras, Kuala Lumpur, to Port Dickson.

bb65dd21dbf96acb: PARIS: World number four Ben Shelton shook off a first-set stumble to beat local favourite Luca Van Assche 5-7 6-3 6-4 and go into the Paris Masters final on Saturday, reaching the third ATP 1000 final of his career.

But the third seed, who was undone by his 17 unforced errors in the first set, found his rhythm in the second. He dragged the 22-year-old Frenchman into long rallies to force mistakes and broke to go 4-2 up, a lead that secured the set.

Shelton looked shaky early in the third set, landing wide twice as Van Assche took a 3-1 lead with a break. But the American turned the tide back in his favour, winning the next four games while Van Assche struggled with double faults and netted forehands.

The 24-year-old is the first American to reach the Paris Masters final since Jack Sock won it in 2017. Shelton will hope to clinch his third ATP 1000 title on Sunday, having won the Canadian Open twice.

2d037e31a79b9504: LEEDS, England: Tottenham Hotspur fans raged after Leeds United's Jayden Bogle escaped a red card for a careless challenge on Mathys Tel that injured the French forward on Saturday, but boss Roberto De Zerbi refused to blame his side's 1-0 Premier League defeat on the decision.

"I have a big confidence in the referee, nothing changes if he (Brooks) goes to watch the clip or not, I think. The departure of Tel seemed to rob Spurs of some of their momentum and De Zerbi said his players were off the pace for the remainder of the game.

"I'm sorry for the result but first of all, I'm sorry for the performance in the second half - we didn't play like a top team, we played without the right spirit, the right character, the right physicality in the duels."
Leeds manager Daniel Farke was delighted with his side's first league win since September, and said that Bogle's clash with Tel was not intentional.
"It's a very unlucky outcome that Mathys is injured and we wish him all the best and he can recover quickly," Farke said.

0d8cd06ceda2dfb0: ASUNCION: Paraguayan prosecutors on Saturday began questioning former president Santiago Pena over his alleged involvement in a banking crisis over which he was impeached a day earlier, a police source confirmed to AFP.

The prosecutor in charge of the probe, Christian Benitez, said that Pena could be formally charged as early as Saturday afternoon.
Senators voted unanimously on Friday to remove Paraguay's youngest-ever president from office, three days after the implosion of Ueno Bank, one of the country's biggest lenders.
The bank's collapse left millions of people locked out of their accounts.
Pena, who had ties to the group that controlled the bank, had offered his resignation.
But lawmakers pressed ahead with impeachment proceedings in order to strip him of the political immunity he would have enjoyed had he stepped down.

ac30c3ff268d6e3d: Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.
This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.

I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.

That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.
There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder.
Hey, thanks for having me, man.

I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.

October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.

You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.
A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.
I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?

It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.

Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.

The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s-
That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ’90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster.

I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now.

It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible.

You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties.

You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now.

Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s.

That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that.

There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing.

All this stuff is falling apart because of AI, because the skillset issue is that now script kiddies have a bunch of the skillset of the Dave Vitales and the other cyber gods who could do these things, such that with this Mac that’s sitting on my desktop, I can reverse engineer a Microsoft patch and walk through and then write stable exploit code. It’s not quite there yet to be automatic. You still have to have a bunch of skills, but we’re really, really close.

What’s really concerning, and what you see with the ARTEX stuff, is you can now kind of let loose on the operational side. We were never secure. It was all a fantasy. These vulnerabilities have always existed. These companies have never been safe. And that is what we’ve seen over the last decade is these mostly Russian ransomware actors nailing the mid-size companies that most people have never heard of that are actually really important, like some midsize industrial company that makes some widget that we all depend upon. I once did work for the largest distributor of medical and dental supplies in the country, and they got really hit badly by a Russian ransomware actor and then dental offices across the country were canceling appointments. Didn’t even make the news, but it was because they couldn’t get gloves, because they couldn’t get supplies. It’s because a company like that’s got one security guy and a 10 person, 12 person IT team and they’re going up against a 20 person Russian ransomware team, they’re toast.

But it’s just because there’s only a handful of Russian teams that could do that. Now two or three Russian kids can have a whole bank of Macs or, if they have the money, they can buy Nvidia H-100s and they can run a ton of agents who do this all day and that is what is changing.

I’m sorry, you asked who was doing this. For Binance, it’s North Koreans and they have an entire team where all they do is steal Bitcoin. Other people have gotten out of it because it’s really hard to compete against a foreign intelligence agency that recruits their smartest kids and all they do is steal Bitcoin. They’re extremely good at it. And for the Binance hack, we could talk about it. There’s probably some AI component, but mostly that was actually human intelligence and very, very smart social engineering and the North Koreans are… I mean, you have to give it to them. They’re very, very good at that.

But for the other stuff, it looks like for the people who are breaking into the AI companies is what’s called the Chinese cottage access industry, which are small Chinese contractors who break into companies and then sell the information to much larger Chinese companies.

That diffusion of skill changing the economics of cyber is really fascinating to me. We ran a headline ages ago called “Attack of the Killer Script Kiddies” at the very beginning of all this, and I feel bad because it is much more suited to now than it was to then, because then it was just a lot of automated mischief. Now —
Because you wasted the headline. You wish you held it back.

We wasted the headline. Every now and again you get a lightning bolt of a headline. You got to get it out there. It’s a great piece of art. We’ll put it in the show notes, but it feels like the diffusion you’re talking about is not that a bunch of teenagers are going to be even more malicious. It’s a bunch of bad actors with real incentives to do harm are now vastly more capable than they were before. And that doesn’t seem like you can re-jigger the economics of that unless you somehow make it really expensive to do the attacks.
I think it’s going to be extremely hard to make it expensive to do the attacks.

We’re going to have to lower the cost of defense. You’re completely right to look at this economic problem because what’s happening is attacks are becoming agentic. The cost per token for attackers is going towards zero, and the cost of defense for defenders is staying quite high. It is very important for us to find ways for defenders to have cheaper options. I think that is critical. That’s something I am personally extremely focused on. To be frank, very few people are.

There are a couple of problems here. One, there’s a ton of focus on the defensive side of AI on finding and fixing bugs. That’s great. It’s important. But software security as a CISO… I work for an AI software company, Cognition. Even as a CISO of a software product company, software security is 25% of my job. I have all kinds of other responsibilities. And software security is the part of my job that has been both the most revolutionized and the most improved by AI. The other 75% has been helped a bit and in some cases made much worse. There’s so much more we need to do than just hill climb on finding and fixing bugs. There’s been so much less hill climbing on all these other things. And the next area needs to be the operational security side.
Wait, give me an example of the other things, the 75%.

Okay. So the operational security side is watching your logs, saying, “Ah, somebody is running our techs against us. I am now going to trigger an investigation. I am going to look to see what is going on and I’m going to make an intelligent decision of what I am going to do to respond to this without shutting down the entire company.” That is SOC (security operations center) work. Companies that want to survive this era are going to have to replace human beings who do that work with the first tier and then eventually the second tier with AI. And you can do that with current LLMs.

The first tier actually has to be not an LLM. It has to be something much dumber because you’re looking at terabytes or petabytes of logs and it is just completely uneconomical to do that with an actual LLM. We have other things — TF-IDFs, MLBERTs, traditional classifiers — that can operate much faster, but then that sets off an alarm and then you send it to a small LLM and then the small LLM calls its bigger brother and that might call an even bigger brother.

But for those models, we need to do a lot more work to optimize them and we need to make them cheap. I have a colleague who works at one of the large security platform companies who said that doing an investigation on one of the big frontier model cyber models costs $900 on their product to do an investigation. That is not going to work when the Russian ransomware guys are either using Macs or they’re using throwaway crypto mining rigs and their marginal cost is zero.

This is one of the things we’re working on at Cognition: We train our own models, retrain open weights, and we’re trying to drive this cost way down. It’s something we’ve done, but we have a lot more work to do here and a lot of other people have work to do here. This is where, as an industry, we have to focus on the Pareto frontier between cost and efficiency on cyber because it’s not just bug-finding.

The other place here is, people talk about Mythos. Mythos is great, Astra Cyber is great. They’re incredible models, but even the people who have access to it, which is a tiny number of companies, they only scan their most important code. And there are hundreds of billions of lines of code out there that are not the Linux kernel, that are the crap C# and J2E code that was written by Infosys 15 years ago. All of that code is not going to go through a frontier cyber model that costs a gazillion dollars. That’s the kind of stuff that we need to work on cost efficiency for.

It feels like you’re describing this cliche that I hear all the time: Everything’s going to get so much worse before it gets totally secure forever. And it doesn’t seem like the model you’re describing leads to that result. We’re not going to fix all the bugs forever in some valley of despair and then always have perfect code. At some point, there’s some cost advantage to the attacker, always. You’re running a company, you can’t write defense that has zero marginal costs. Someone has to do it even if the attackers are so infinite that their marginal cost is effectively zero. So are we going to go through a period where everything is so much worse and then it’s perfect forever? Or how does the cost manage itself out, into balance?
0f0e00fd4a24ced0: Fireworks AI is fine with helping companies run AI models in their own datacenters, though VP Rob Ferguson argues against doing so.

Ferguson told The Register in an interview that while Fireworks AI, a managed inference provider, supports on-prem AI, "we're trying to push people more and more away from it because frankly, it's just the economics."
The GPU hardware is just so expensive that if you can't keep it fully utilized, it's a waste of money, he contends. Ten thousand GPUs, he said, represent a billion dollars of capital.
"You don't want those things to be sitting idle," he said.

For companies with particularly sensitive workloads, Ferguson said, Fireworks is happy to work something out – it offers a service called Sovereign for just that purpose and it has partners like Microsoft that can help. But most inference work probably doesn't need that level of protection, he said.

"The state of the art for everyone is to have a portfolio of models," he explained. "In fact, I think most people don't know that the best model in the world's not Astra. The best model in the world's not Fable. The best model is literally a portfolio and we can prove it. You are always better routing between a few models than to do one singular model."

That's what Fireworks does through Nexus and its API, alongside competitors like Together AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra. As a managed inference platform, Fireworks AI routes inference tasks to whichever model, frontier model subscription, or API is best suited to handle them.
But the company is not just doing naive routing like an AI gateway. It's evaluating tasks as they come in and directing them to the optimal model.

"We build custom routers," Ferguson explained. "Our auto model is continuously updating so that we actually go through and we grade the difficulty of the task and we see if there're affinities that the models have, like Kimi is slightly better at JavaScript than Python, things like this."
The company's competitive edge, he contends, is its crack engineering team, which follows from its founders' work on PyTorch, a widely used open source machine learning library.

"We're performance experts both on the training and inference side," he explained. "People I think don't understand how important, for example, numerics is. So when you use a model, it's always called a mixture of experts – an expert is a different machine.

"And so you have all these different machines. It actually matters when you're training that you go back to precisely the right machine, because if you don't, the other machine will still answer the question, but it'll answer in a slightly different way. So we have to know how to build the topology to write back the data to the right space. We have to understand floating point precision [to handle very small values]. We have to be able to do all this where we're routing through a complex fabric through potentially more than one provider depending on what everything is. And so we're really systems experts."

Hyperscalers, he argues, will give you a GPU but then it's your responsibility to put it to use. Fireworks' advantage involves being able to maximize utilization at scale while maintaining model precision and speed.
Ferguson said AI keeps coming back to economics.

"People are just trying to figure out more and more things to use AI for and [to answer questions like] just how much more can I send to cached models, how much more can I send to open models, when do I need this specialization?" he said. "So we're constantly working with customers to help them come up with their own evaluation criteria."

One reason for this, Ferguson explained, is that frontier model companies are not transparent about their caching rates. He said Fireworks was working with a data science company and was caching about 90 percent of the tasks.

"We looked at [Anthropic's] Opus and it was caching 30 percent of the time," he said. "It was doing AI rework constantly. And with AI, rework is by far your biggest cost. If it's not hitting a cache, then your costs are absolutely insane. And so the token cost is not the real cost. It's the cost per task. And they're hiding that from you. And so we always tell our customers to be tracking cost per task, because that's the real number."
Another factor that companies should consider in their cost calculations, Ferguson suggested, is the value of their data and whether they're giving that data away for training.
"I think people grossly underestimate the value of their data," he said.

Fireworks AI has a zero data-retention policy, "but a lot of times," Ferguson said, "these other companies [do] not, and you should be getting paid for your data. Nobody really knew at the beginning of this current era that these models are memorizers. But now there's plenty of evidence that these models are. So if they're going to be using your data, then you should be getting value for it."
But it's not just about cost. Speed, said Ferguson, is underappreciated.

"Speed is the thing that people often don't know they can ask for," he said. "It's such a game changer for me and how I work with AI is so different when the responses come back as fast as I ask them."
What's the advantage of model ensembling, as the company refers to its model routing activities? A bill that's at least 50 percent smaller, Ferguson claims.

"So we say six to eight times cheaper," he said. "The reality is that because a lot of folks have a preference in their tooling, we kinda guarantee that in the case where you're still using a combo of closed and open models, we can always guarantee that your bill will drop by half right away. Like we're sure about that. And then the question is can we just get you to use more stuff?" ®
6621c3079ee1422e: KUALA LUMPUR: A two-hour-long downpour triggered flash floods in Kampung Melayu Subang, with the Jalan Jati Bridge spanning Sungai Damansara closed due to erosion along the riverbank.

Selangor Fire and Rescue Department Operations Division Assistant Director Ashrul Riezal Asbar said the flash floods were caused by the overflow of the drainage system, and not by the phenomenon of unusually high tides.
"Heavy rain this evening caused the drainage system to be overwhelmed by the volume of water, but water levels in the affected areas are now reported to be receding," he said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the Selangor Public Works Department, in a separate statement, said the Jalan Jati Bridge in Section U6, Kampung Melayu Subang, had been closed to all vehicles for safety reasons following severe erosion of the bridge abutment structure.
The department said the erosion and embankment collapse occurred following a rise in water levels and strong currents in Sungai Damansara due to continuous heavy rain.

"A Traffic Management Plan has been implemented to regulate vehicle movement, and road users are advised to use the alternative route via Lorong Cempaka and comply with the diversion signs at the location," the department said.

The department would also carry out temporary repair works in the affected area, subject to site safety conditions and the availability of materials from quarries, as the work would take place during a public holiday period.

For the long term, the department said an allocation would be sought to carry out permanent repairs to the bridge abutment structure and reinforce the banks of Sungai Damansara to ensure the stability of the bridge.
6bec1185864bba78: LEEDS: Leeds rode their luck to beat in-form Tottenham 1-0 on Saturday, benefiting from a controversial decision to allow Jayden Bogle to stay on the pitch after an ugly tackle on Mathys Tel.
Substitute Noah Okafor was the match-winner, making an almost immediate impact after being introduced by Leeds boss Daniel Farke in the 77th minute.
The home team started brightly, and Spurs breathed a sigh of relief in the early minutes when VAR ruled that Mateus Fernandes had not handled the ball in the penalty area.
As the first half wore on, the visitors established themselves, though clear chances were at a premium.
Leeds got the benefit of a contentious decision about 10 minutes before the break when Bogle caught Tel's trailing ankle with his studs, leaving the Tottenham winger writhing on the ground in pain.
After a lengthy VAR check, no action was taken against Bogle, who was not even booked for the challenge, but Tel was forced off a few minutes later, hobbling off to be replaced by Dominic Solanke.
Leeds had two big chances early in the second half as Dominic Calvert-Lewin's header was blocked by Solanke before Nico Elvedi nodded wide on the follow-up.
Calvert-Lewin then burst forward again but opted to pass to Ao Tanaka rather than shooting, and the Japanese international skied his shot.
Leeds were now on the front foot, and Antonin Kinsky produced a wonderful stop after Sean Longstaff's swivel and shot.
But they got the goal their pressure deserved in the 79th minute.
Harry Wilson, another substitute, controlled the ball and played it into the path of Okafor, who gave Kinsky no chance.
Spurs came agonisingly close to an equaliser but goalkeeper James Trafford made a brilliant save from Jan Paul van Hecke's header.
The result ends Tottenham's run of three straight league wins, while it was the first victory in six games for Leeds, who climbed to eighth in the table.
fffd34efe24ea1c8: PETALING JAYA: The National Security Council (MKN) has warned the public against claims of cyberattacks against Malaysia being spread on social media and said national cybersecurity remains under control, with the national cyber threat level remaining at a moderate level.

The council said the National Cyber Security Agency and the national cyber coordination and command centre continually monitored any threats to cybersecurity and had taken note of cybersecurity incidents and system disruptions involving several financial institutions, Bernama reported.
“Bank Negara Malaysia is implementing comprehensive and integrated preparedness measures, including continuous monitoring of the cybersecurity status of the critical information infrastructure.
"Efforts were being made to ensure that any threats are detected and addressed promptly, while essential services continue to operate smoothly,” the council said in a statement.
Late on Friday, Bank Rakyat shut off access to its website after its web page was defaced. In response, communications minister Fahmi Fadzil said banking institutions in the country remained safe.

The MKN statement came hours after social media users were reported to have expressed concerns about cyberattacks from abroad, with reports of counter-attacks allegedly being launched from Malaysia, Sinar Harian reported.

Social media users have spread images of a "Live Threat Map" from the US-based cybersecurity company FortiGuard Labs showing several locations, including Cyberjaya, Shah Alam, and Petaling Jaya, as areas where cyber-threat activities had been recorded.

The map lists Malaysia in 18th place among the top 20 countries targeted for cyberattacks, with 1.8 million attacks recorded over the past 24 hours. Threat activity is shown as originating from various countries, including France, Bulgaria, Indonesia, Japan, and China, with threat levels categorised as "critical" or "high".

Much of the displayed activity is believed to involve attempts to breach web servers and internet routers used in homes and offices, the report said. Social media users also noted claims of retaliatory actions, including posts about a person in Batu Pahat, Johor, purportedly involved in such activities until the early hours of the morning.

Italy's foreign minister Antonio Tajani said his personal information had been leaked on the dark web by cybercriminals who were seeking further details about him and his family, exposing them to "new threats and intimidation".
In a post on X, Tajani said the perpetrators had been circulating his data for days and were offering to pay for additional information about him and his loved ones, the Turkish news agency reported.

Tajani linked the alleged targeting to Italy's support for Ukraine. He also suggested that the threats were partly a response to cybersecurity measures introduced at the Italian foreign ministry in recent months.
ce8c421a4f24917b: PARIS: Tens of thousands of people were set to protest across France on Saturday in a new show of anger against the government with Paris police imposing strict security to prevent an unauthorised gathering close to the Elysee Palace.

The protests mark the fourth weekend in a row of demonstrations, which have burst on the scene as the country tilts towards presidential elections in five months' time in which the far right sees its best chance yet to win power.
Authorities expected up to 170,000 people to protest nationwide, including 60,000 in Paris. The demonstrations come two days after mass protests by unions on Nov 5 accompanied by strikes.
Some 70,000 members of the security forces were deployed Saturday, ready to move in quickly after mass protests on Oct 17 degenerated into the worst riots seen in France in years.
Unions planned to stage a march along a traditional route, from the Place de la Republique in central Paris to Place de la Nation in the east of the city.

But the Yellow Vests movement – a group whose protests shook President Emmanuel Macron in the early years of his rule almost a decade ago – has called for a rival demonstration at the Place de la Concorde in central Paris, a stone's throw from the Elysee Palace where the president resides and from the lower house of parliament.
This action has been banned by the authorities, and on Saturday morning a large police presence was visible in the vicinity to prevent protesters getting close.
Paris police said they had carried out more than 840 checks on individuals at train stations in Paris and its inner suburbs by late morning.

Protest marches were already underway in cities from Marseille in the south, Bordeaux in the southwest and Lille in the north, AFP reporters said. Meanwhile, shop windows of stores in Paris and other cities were again barricaded with wooden shutters to prevent ransacking.

"The risk is exactly the same as on previous Saturdays," said interior minister Laurent Nunez, calling on authorities "not to lower their guard in the face of more fragmented – or even sporadic – incidents, where the level of violence will not diminish in intensity".
"If there are any rioters or looters... we'll be ready and waiting for them," he said.
'Mass disobedience'
The Yellow Vests movement called for its banned rally to go ahead in a show of defiance to what it viewed as an attempt to suppress the French right to protest.
"We are calling for mass disobedience," said Benjamin Ball, a member of its coordinating committee.

The wave of demonstrations was sparked by a movement in late September by high school students angered by conditions at their establishments. These teens, joined by university students, remain at the heart of the protests.
The police response has faced criticism for being heavy-handed, with dozens of internal investigations launched into allegations of brutality against demonstrators.
After several instances of apparent police brutality against AFP reporters covering the protests, the international news agency on Friday urged protection for its journalists.
The government is grappling with ways to find solutions but is constrained by France's gigantic debt pile, which is already spooking markets.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu was to hold a meeting with unions and employer federation representatives on Monday to discuss wages and purchasing power.

"The only thing that will bring the protests to an end is a response to the demands that have been put forward for several weeks by workers, civil servants, young people and pensioners," an inter-union coalition said on Friday.

Student and teacher groups in France have called for a new strike on Tuesday to keep pressure on the government for more education spending, saying they were "in a position of strength (and) the government in a position of weakness and starting to yield".

Polls, meanwhile, show that far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the favourite to win the Elysee in 2027, with her main rival currently not one of Macron's centrist former allies but hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon. Melenchon was due to address a rally later Saturday.

ec4c9aebddfebadf: PETALING JAYA: Sembilan individu ditahan dalam siasatan kes pembunuhan seorang remaja lelaki berusia 19 tahun, yang dipercayai ditikam dalam pergaduhan di Sibu, Sarawak.
Ketua Polis Sibu, Abang Zainal Abidin Abang Ahmad, berkata suspek yang berusia antara 16 hingga 42 tahun ditahan hasil risikan dan siasatan Jabatan Siasatan Jenayah, lapor Berita Harian.
Seorang remaja dilaporkan maut selepas dipercayai ditikam pada bahagian dada dengan senjata tajam dalam kejadian kira-kira 12 tengah malam.
Mangsa meninggal dunia selepas dibawa ke hospital untuk mendapatkan rawatan kecemasan.
Polis menerima laporan berhubung kejadian pergaduhan yang menyaksikan pengadu dipukul sekumpulan individu, pada kira-kira 2 pagi tadi.
Kes disiasat mengikut Seksyen 302 Kanun Keseksaan kerana membunuh, yang memperuntukkan hukuman mati atau penjara antara 30 hingga 40 tahun serta sebatan tidak kurang 12 kali, jika sabit kesalahan.

2839734cd56a51ea: KUALA LUMPUR: National development should not be measured solely by the grandeur of skyscrapers, technological advancements or an influx of investments, said Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.
He said it must be anchored in the development of individuals who are civilised, possess good character and hold noble human values.
Anwar said efforts to build a great nation must begin with the establishment of happy family institutions.

"Families are the foundation of society and pillar of national strength, and as such, the concept of 'Menggapai di Langit, Mengakar di Bumi' (Reaching for the sky, Rooted in Ground) should serve as a guiding principle in educating the younger generation to master technology and new knowledge without neglecting values, manners, compassion and noble character.

"I am confident that efforts to build a great nation must begin with building happy families, because it is from the family institution that generations who will determine the face and future of the nation emerge," he said in a Facebook post.

The prime minister said the Madani Government would continue to strengthen policies and initiatives prioritising family well-being, including the welfare of mothers and children, childcare facilities, support for persons with disabilities (PwDs) and recognition of the role of caregivers.

Earlier, Anwar officiated the National Family Month 2026 celebration in Shah Alam, Selangor, today, which was also attended by his wife, Datuk Seri Dr Wan Azizah Wan Ismail, and Minister of Women, Family and Community Development Datuk Seri Nancy Shukri.

At the same time, the prime minister also commended Nancy and her ministry for successfully organising the celebration and their steadfast commitment to championing women's well-being and strengthening the family institution as a cornerstone of societal and national development.
0165371845b1d7ec: LUSAIL: Marco Bezzecchi on Saturday grabbed pole position for the Qatar Grand Prix after setting the fastest time in qualifying ahead of championship leader Marc Marquez.
As the sun began to set over the dusty Lusail Circuit, the Italian on an Aprilia broke the Qatar track record with a time of 1 minute 50.028 seconds.
He outclassed all his rivals, including Ducati's Marquez, who could win an eighth world title in the premier class on Sunday.
The Catalan rider and Italian Fabio Di Giannantonio, on a Ducati VR46, had dominated Friday's qualifying sessions but were left 0.266 sec and 0.299 sec behind Bezzecchi.
Bezzecchi, who is third in the standings, will attempt to delay the seven-time world champion's title clinch this weekend.
The other Aprilia rider, Jorge Martin, second behind Marquez in the standings, made his return after suffering a broken right wrist and qualified 11th.
290c7ec63ac5f2d3: Myanmar's military-appointed election commission has scheduled by-elections for April next year to fill dozens of parliamentary seats, state media said on Friday, including in areas impacted by a protracted civil war.
The contest for vacant seats in 55 constituencies will be held on April 4, the Global New Light of Myanmar reported.
The vote follows a general election held in December and January that was won overwhelmingly by the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party in the absence of any viable opposition.
The election was criticised as a sham by the United Nations and many Western countries and led to junta chief Min Aung Hlaing becoming president.
The USDP currently controls 84% of the bicameral parliament.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since a 2021 coup triggered a civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.
Several seats in the by-election will encompass townships in the Sagaing Region plus Chin and Shan states, where anti-military resistance forces have a strong presence.
Not included is restive Rakhine state, bordering Bangladesh, where the military is locked in fierce fighting with the rebel Arakan Army.
Voting in the general election was held in 692 constituencies, with 121 excluded as they were out of the military's control.
7f861891db48e9fc: PETALING JAYA: Heavy rain since this afternoon has flooded several areas in Seberang Perai Tengah, Penang, while two trees toppled by the storm crushed vehicles.
Bernama reported that the Seberang Perai Tengah disaster management committee identified Seberang Jaya, Permatang Rawa, Tanah Liat, Mengkuang Titi and Jalan Baru as affected areas.
It said the situation remained under control, though several houses were flooded and drainage issues were reported in Seberang Jaya.

The Penang fire and rescue department said the two trees had fallen in Perai and Mengkuang Titi. No casualties were reported in either incident, in which a taxi was crushed in Perai and a Perodua Bezza in Mengkuang Titi.
236acdea3dd25631: GAZA CITY: Heavy rain on Saturday flooded tens of thousands of displaced people's tents in war-devastated Gaza, Palestinian authorities said, leaving them without shelter.
In a statement, the Hamas-run government media office said that about "70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day" of rains.
It also noted the "collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries", some critical, in various areas of the tiny territory.
Since early Saturday, hundreds of displaced families have been seen fleeing camps in parts of Gaza City and in the central and northern areas of the Strip after they were inundated by rainwater.

Civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal told AFP his teams had received more than 1,500 calls during the night from residents requesting urgent assistance after their tents were flooded, explaining that the agency "is operating without any equipment or capabilities".

"We have issued an urgent distress call to the international community and humanitarian organisations to intervene immediately to save hundreds of thousands of displaced people from the flooding of their tents."
"We cannot face the consequences of this storm on our own."

Um Muhammad al-Hersh, 45, who lives with her family in a tent in western Gaza, told AFP: "We were not able to save the mattresses, and all the clothes were soaked. Our suffering is repeated every winter."
Maryam Odeh, 34, who lives with her children in Deir al-Balah, said, "We no longer know how to protect our children. My children ask me where we will sleep tonight, and I have no answer."
For his part, Khaled al-Najjar, 41, said, "We fear for our children not only from the flooding of the tents but also from the cold and the widespread diseases."

A coalition of Palestinian civil society organisations warned in a statement of "the catastrophe that has come to threaten the lives of hundreds of thousands of residents", pointing to the risk of the spread of diseases and epidemics.
The coalition, which includes dozens of local institutions and organisations, called for "pressure on Israel to allow the entry of humanitarian aid without restrictions".
A fragile ceasefire came into effect on Oct 10, 2025, after two years of war that erupted following the unprecedented attack carried out by Hamas on Israel on Oct 7, 2023.
Despite the ceasefire agreement reached with Egyptian, Qatari, and American mediation, the Israeli army continues airstrikes and ground operations on an almost daily basis.

Mustafa Qazzaat, a member of the Gaza city council and an official in the Strip's emergency committee, said Israel has not allowed prefabricated homes to shelter the displaced in Gaza since the truce was announced and has only permitted the entry of limited numbers of tents.

Qazzaat told AFP on Saturday that Gaza "needs 200,000 prefabricated homes urgently, in addition to the entry of heavy machinery to remove the rubble of destroyed homes and buildings, open main roads, and urgently provide electricity and heating".
3bc90bae669e3a6f: SIBU: Police have detained nine people, aged between 16 and 42, to assist a probe into the murder of a 19-year-old who is believed to have been stabbed during a fight at a public park in Jalan Gambir here early today.

Sibu district police chief ACP Abang Zainal Abidin Abang Ahmad said all suspects were rounded up at several locations around Sibu between 10am and 4pm today following intelligence gathering and investigations by the Sibu police headquarters' Criminal Investigation Department (CID).
He said police received a report at about 2am regarding a brawl where the complainant was assaulted by a group of people.
"During the incident, a young man was believed to have been stabbed with a sharp weapon and was confirmed dead by a medical team from Sibu Hospital," he said in a statement.
Abang Zainal Abidin said the incident had also gone viral on social media.

He said the case is being investigated under Section 302 of the Penal Code for murder, which provides for the death penalty or imprisonment of between 30 and 40 years, and not less than 12 strokes of the cane, upon conviction.
Police have also urged members of the public with information on the incident to come forward to assist in the investigation.
1c63b92f1a484eb8: PETALING JAYA: Police have arrested nine people aged between 16 and 42 years old to assist in an investigation into the murder of a 19-year-old boy, believed to have been stabbed in a brawl at a public park in Sibu early this morning.

084c3fdfc95bbe67: KUALA LUMPUR: Majlis Keselamatan Negara (MKN) menegaskan bahawa situasi keselamatan siber negara berada dalam keadaan terkawal dengan Tahap Ancaman Keselamatan Siber Negara (NCTL) kekal pada tahap sederhana.
Agensi Keselamatan Siber Negara (Nacsa) memaklumkan Pusat Kawalan dan Penyelarasan Siber Negara (NC4) sedang memantau situasi keselamatan siber secara berterusan susulan perkembangan terkini.

Nacsa mengambil maklum mengenai insiden keselamatan siber serta gangguan sistem yang melibatkan beberapa institusi kewangan dan sedang bekerjasama rapat dengan pihak berkaitan bagi memantau perkembangan.

"Bank Negara selaku ketua sektor perbankan dan kewangan sedang melaksanakan langkah kesiapsiagaan yang menyeluruh dan bersepadu termasuklah pemantauan berterusan perkembangan tahap keselamatan siber entiti infrastruktur maklumat kritikal negara (NCII) di bawahnya.

"NACSA turut bekerjasama dengan ketua sektor dan entiti NCII bagi memastikan sebarang ancaman dapat dikesan dan ditangani dengan segera, serta perkhidmatan penting negara terus beroperasi dengan lancar," menurut kenyataan.

253d41ddcf6d6287: JAKARTA: Hundreds of workers rallied in support of Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto on Saturday amid allegations that police illegally wiretapped him, while hundreds of women marched against the president's policies.

The pro-Prabowo demonstration marked a contrast to recent protests against his administration, part of growing public discontent over his costly populist policies, handling of raging wildfires and weakening investor confidence in Southeast Asia's biggest economy.

Labour Party Chairperson Said Iqbal, leading the workers' rally, called for unity to support Prabowo and said he would mobilise union members against those who threaten the former general's presidency.

"We can mobilise members of our organisation across every town, every factory," Said, a special adviser to the president, was quoted as saying by Detik News. "We are prepared to respond at any moment to maintain order should any unrest arise, whether instigated by foreign interests or by individuals seeking to cause trouble."

Indonesian police have named four senior police officials as suspects accused of attempting to intercept Prabowo's communications, including a former police chief who is known as a loyalist of former president Joko Widodo.
The scandal has exposed deepening cracks between Prabowo and his predecessor and former backer, known as Jokowi.
Jokowi has said he respected the legal process. The lawyer for one of the four suspects said his client would cooperate with the investigation.

Also on Saturday, civil society groups held the women's march in Jakarta to demand more women's rights and protest against Prabowo's handling of the forest fires that have been raging for months, his costly free-meal programme and a tax on women's sanitary products.
There have been several protests launched against Prabowo in recent months, including student rallies last week in the capital and other cities. — REUTERS

2bf0f02a2a6424d3: ALOR GAJAH: For Barisan Nasional candidate for Gadek S. Nadarajah, this Deepavali will be unlike previous celebrations as his campaign commitments leave little time for family gatherings.
With the Melaka election campaign taking priority, even a planned lunch with his family remains uncertain as he continues making his rounds to meet voters.
As MIC's sole candidate in the election, Nadarajah said his focus was on engaging with voters, listening to their concerns and understanding issues affecting their daily lives.
He said he had only managed to call his father this morning to check on the family's Deepavali preparations.
"My focus is entirely on campaigning. I only managed to call my father this morning to ask about the family's Deepavali preparations.
"He told me everything was in order and that I should not worry about things at home.
"I told them perhaps they could come and meet me for lunch tomorrow, but even that has not been confirmed because I do not know where I will be at that time," he said when met while campaigning here.
Instead of spending time with his family, Nadarajah plans to visit temples and the homes of Indian voters in Gadek.
"Tomorrow, I will visit several temples in Gadek where the Hindu community will be celebrating Deepavali.

cf0823c342f8f6e8: LOS ANGELES, Nov 7 — One of the world’s most popular fan fiction libraries has been dark for over a week after a cyberattack forced it offline, leaving millions of fans without access to their favourite stories.
Since October 29, anyone trying to reach Archive of Our Own — known to devotees as AO3 — has been met with a message saying the site is down for maintenance.
“It’s all over my social feed. People are in withdrawal,” Johanna Sarriot, a writer and co-founder of pop-up romance bookstore Love Love Books in Los Angeles, told AFP.
Fan fiction refers to stories written by amateur authors using characters and worlds from already-existing books, films or TV shows.
Contributors rewrite endings, invent romances or give minor characters their own adventures, then share them online for free.

Once a niche hobby, it has become a launchpad for the publishing industry, generating breakout smashes like E.L. James’s Fifty Shades of Grey, which began as Twilight fan fiction, and Ali Hazelwood’s bestseller The Love Hypothesis, which sprang from the Star Wars universe.
Launched in 2008, AO3 has become the genre’s main home, with more than 11 million registered users and nearly 18 million works stored on the platform.
In 2019, it won a Hugo Award for Best Related Work, one of science fiction’s most prestigious prizes.

“We wanted to make sure that there was a place for fans to engage in non-commercial creativity in ways that wouldn’t barrage them with ads, censor them to placate advertisers, sell their data, or do anything but provide a space for fandom,” said Harvard Law School professor Rebecca Tushnet, who helped found the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW) which runs the site.
‘AO3 is not gone’
Romance fans have been among the hardest hit by the outage.
“Romance readers read really fast and they read a lot,” explained Sarriot.
For the bookseller, what is at stake goes beyond a website. Fan fiction is where many future authors learn their craft and where readers discover new writers.
“Writers who were able to cut their teeth on fanfiction, and just write as much as they wanted with all the joy and no constraints, can lead to really great novels,” she said.
OTW says it does not believe the user database, which holds usernames, email addresses and encrypted passwords, was stolen, but cannot rule it out.
“AO3 is not gone! There is no data loss and we look forward to restoring the site as soon as possible,” Tushnet added.
The non-profit says it hopes to have things up and running again within a month.
For web developer Yohan Mebrouk, the timeline is a sign of how serious the attack was.
The delay could reflect limited resources, he explained, or the need for a full software upgrade, which he called “an enormous job”.
Well-run sites keep backup copies of their databases, he added. “If they did things right, everyone will get everything back.”
In the meantime, Sarriot is happy to point stranded readers elsewhere.
“Come to Love Love Books and check out a romance novel!” she said, pointing to her shelves full of paperbacks. — AFP
16a91ca9fca2c937: WASHINGTON, Nov 7 — Production of Cybertrucks — the pickups hailed by enthusiasts as a symbol of Elon Musk’s futuristic ambitions and equally hated as ugly reminders of the Donald Trump era — will wind down, the Tesla CEO said yesterday.
Tesla will stop building the truck at its Texas factory around the middle of 2027 to free up space for its Cybercab robotaxi, Musk said.
“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk wrote on X.
Musk did not say whether the truck would be built elsewhere or discontinued altogether, nor what would happen to outstanding orders.
Wes Morrill, the Cybertruck’s lead engineer, wrote in a separate post that the truck “was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab.”
“Thanks to everyone who contributed to making the future (look) like the future,” he added.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Tesla Cybertruck electric vehicles sit parked in a storage lot in San Diego, California on April 11, 2025. — AFP pic
Tesla fans lamented the departure of the Cybertruck on X, the social media platform Musk owns, but the tycoon reassured them that the Cybertruck fleet “will be around for a long time.”

The truck came to be seen as an extension of Musk himself, and its image became entangled with his politics as he took on a high-profile role leading the Trump administration’s cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency. Some owners reported vandalism and harassment.
The angular stainless-steel behemoth was unveiled in November 2019, and Musk said at the time it had drawn 250,000 preorders within days.
Production was originally slated for 2021 but was repeatedly delayed, with customer deliveries starting in late 2023.
Tesla built its Texas lines with planned capacity of 250,000 trucks a year, but sales have come nowhere near that figure.
As US demand slumped, Tesla began selling the truck abroad, starting deliveries in South Korea in November 2025 and in the United Arab Emirates in January.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Tesla electric cars and a Cybertruck are displayed in a test drive vehicle charging area at a shopping mall parking garage in San Diego, California, on April 23, 2025. — AFP pic
Tesla does not break out Cybertruck revenue, but its “other models” category, which includes the pickup, accounts for just a small percentage of sales.
Cox Automotive estimated total sales of just 72,702, with more than half in 2024 and fading thereafter.
The truck has also been subject to multiple recalls and complaints over build quality.
The Cybercab, a two-seat vehicle with no steering wheel or pedals, was unveiled in October 2024.
Tesla began production at the Texas plant in April and started offering paid Cybercab rides in Austin in September through its existing Robotaxi service.

“The decision to discontinue the Cybertruck highlights how difficult it can be to translate strong initial attention and enthusiasm around a new vehicle into sustainable mainstream demand,” said Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive.
Tesla saw the vehicle as a bid for the giant US pickup truck market, but it quickly became a “niche” product, Valdez Streaty said.

The robotaxi is central to Musk’s effort to recast Tesla as an artificial intelligence and robotics company rather than a carmaker, though its success depends on the company delivering fully driverless technology, which it has yet to demonstrate at scale. — AFP
7f9af3a30b197c1a: JOHOR BAHRU, Nov 7 — Deepavali celebrations are not just about wearing new attire and preparing an array of traditional delicacies, but also about strengthening family bonds and preserving age-old traditions passed down through generations.

For Singaporean P. Parvathy, 65, from Sengkang, a visit to Johor Bahru to shop for Deepavali essentials has become an annual tradition, while also giving her the opportunity to meet relatives living in the state.

Little India in Brickfields bustles with activity as shoppers make a last-minute dash for Deepavali essentials. — Bernama pic

Meanwhile, for housewife K. Kalaivani, 40, from Pasir Gudang, this year’s Deepavali holds special significance as her family will also be holding a religious ceremony to mark her daughter’s coming of age.

Among the items available are tarts, suji and murukku, priced from RM35 per jar, while customers can purchase four jars at a promotional price of RM120.
She said the variety of snacks also complemented the tradition of visiting family and friends, which adds to the festive atmosphere of Deepavali celebrations each year.
Deepavali, also known as the Festival of Lights, will be celebrated tomorrow by Hindus across the country. — Bernama
47c508b29abf64f9: GUA MUSANG, Nov 7 — The joy of celebrating Deepavali knows no bounds, with some residents of Gua Musang willing to travel hundreds of kilometres to other states in search of festive essentials.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that drew a blank, felt the squeeze, played the queen, and made donkey-bull love.

First, scientists shed new light on how Earth ended up losing more than a billion years of its geological record, a puzzle that has resisted explanation for decades. Then: octopuses in tight spots, a topless spear-brandishing Celt, and a tale of unlikely tail.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
“Blank Space” (Earth’s Version)
Dhungana, Santosh and Flament, Nicolas. “The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity. Nature.

Earth doesn’t trouble itself too much with keeping intact archives. With its tectonic activity and erosive forces, our planet is constantly wiping out huge chunks of its own memory, creating gaps in the geological record called unconformities.

The Great Unconformity, the largest gap of this kind, reveals that Earth straight-up deleted more than a billion years of strata, for reasons that remain hotly debated and mysterious. Sandstone that dates back to the Cambrian period some 538 million years is often found directly on top of ancient “basement” rocks that date back anywhere from 1.2 billion to 1.8 billion years ago. This missing layer shows up around the world, hinting that it was erased by a global event.
Now, scientists have placed the origins of the Great Unconformity deep inside Earth’s mantle, during the tectonic tumult of supercontinent breakup.

“The cause or causes of the Great Unconformity are unknown,” said authors Santosh Dhungana and Nicolas Flament of the University of Wollongong. “The proposed mechanisms include extensive glacial erosion during Snowball Earth (about 720–635 million years ago), rifting and plume activity, sea-level fall and mantle-driven dynamic topography.”
“These processes have not been dynamically tested, with limited comparison between global models and global datasets to explain the spatial distribution of the Great Unconformity,” the team added.

To fill the knowledge gap about the geological gap, the researchers ran models of the formation and breakup of ancient supercontinents during the eons preceding the Cambrian period, when complex life rapidly proliferated in Earth’s seas. Massive landmasses were pushed upward by motions in Earth’s mantle during this time. Exposed to erosive forces such as weather, glaciers, and eventually oceans, they became sanded down over time, creating the vast void.

“Our models explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved in North America and show that it is a first-order surface expression of deep geodynamic processes that transformed global landscapes and sediment fluxes,” the team concluded.

Scientists will no doubt continue to debate the cause of this planet-wide memory lapse, but there is consensus that the same mechanisms also set the stage for the emergence of complex life during the Cambrian. No matter what caused the Great Unconformity, we partly owe our existence to it today.
In other news…
Putting the squeeze on octopuses
Xin, Wenci et al. “Overcoming environmental constraints: octopus uses 3-step or 4-step strategies to squeeze through small holes.” Journal of Experimental Biology.

We’ll move now from massive gaps in Earth’s memory to tiny gaps that octopuses can somehow squeeze through. These tentacled escape artists can famously maneuver their way through passages that seem impossibly small relative to their bodies, an ability that has spawned a subgenre of viral videos.

Now, scientists have discovered the secrets of “octopus-squeezing behavior” by observing two species—the common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) and the Mayan octopus (Octopus maya)—navigating small holes in laboratory containers.

“Our study demonstrates that octopuses employ two primary strategies, 3-step and 4-step, for squeezing through narrow spaces,” said researchers led by Wenci Xin of the National University of Singapore. “The key distinction between these strategies lies in whether the body is squeezed separately from the arms.”

The first two steps were probing the aperture and then shifting a few arms through it. Navigating the tightest spaces required breaking up the final passage into two parts: Pulling the remaining arms to the other side, and then compressing the mantle behind the head so they could fit through last.
In addition to documenting these amazing feats of flexibility in nature, the study is the perfect excuse to revisit the classic X-Files episode “Squeeze.”
A queen hidden in plain sight?
Russell, Miles. “Verica Rex: Searching for a ‘lost’ queen of the British Iron Age.” Current Archaeology.

When Rome invaded Britain 2,000 years ago, they had the help of an inside man—or was it an inside woman? In a new article, an archaeologist makes the case that the British king Verica, who aided the Roman invasion of their own homeland, was actually a queen that has been misgendered lo these many centuries.

Miles Russell of Bournemouth University argues that Verica was a woman based in part on the leader’s Latin name, which ends in the suffix “a” which is common for women, as opposed to names ending in “-us” for men.

Coins also depict Verica using “slender, bare-breasted equestrian figures that appear irrefutably female in contrast to the overtly masculine warriors on the issues of Iron Age rulers like Tasciovanus and Caratacus,” according to Russell.

Many experts are not convinced that the evidence points to a secret ancient queen, and Verica’s gender is likely to inspire much more debate. Wikipedia, our great public arbiter, has not changed Verica’s male pronouns.

Women leaders weren’t unheard of in Celtic Britain, as evidenced by the queens Cartimandua and Boudica, who lived in the same century as Verica. Regardless of whether Verica was among their ranks, this leader was a consequential figure in the Roman takeover of Britain.
Achille and Patroclo: More than friends
Da Cruz, André B et al. “A socio-sexual bond between a bull and a male donkey.” Current Biology.
Scientists who were conducting fieldwork on monkeys in Ethiopia serendipitously stumbled upon a very different discovery—a tender same-sex relationship between a bull and a donkey.

Achille, a bull, and Patroclo, a donkey, belong to different owners, but they graze together by day. Despite the availability of other males and females in their pasture, this pair has developed a strong socio-sexual bond that includes nuzzling, licking, and Achille sexually mounting Patroclo.

“Patroclo frequently presented his hindquarters toward Achille and nipped him,” said researchers led by André Beirão da Cruz of the University of Pisa. “In the only two instances in which Achille approached and mounted another male donkey, this individual showed clear avoidance behaviours and displayed threatening facial expressions (e.g. ear flattening), which were never observed in Patroclo during the 51 mountings (34 with intromission) with Achille.”

Same-sex sexual behavior is extremely common in nature and has a wide variety of possible explanations, including social cohesion, mistaken identity, or lack of access to opposite-sex mates. But what Achille and Patroclo have is special. Despite being different species and having alternate mating options, the pair share a highly selective and reciprocal social and sexual bond.

“Although interpreting this behaviour is challenging, the mounting attempts, taken together with the repeated and mutual affiliative interactions between the two animals, may signal the quality of their relationship” and “the strength of the animals’ social bond,” the team concluded.

In addition to this heartwarming tale, the study goes to show that you never know what you might find when you chase your goals. The researchers were there to watch geladas, but it turned out those primates weren’t the only animals monkeying around.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.
639e141f46a5c632: FRANKFURT: The son of the ousted shah of Iran on Saturday received a "Freedom Prize" in Frankfurt awarded to the Iranian people in a ceremony that critics said was illegitimate.

Greeted by thousands of demonstrators chanting their support and waving pre-revolutionary Iranian flags, Reza Pahlavi took receipt of the prize awarded by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, an activist group close to the liberal FDP party.

Iran "is a country not waiting to be taught democracy, this is a country being prevented from practising it," Pahlavi said at St Paul's Church, famous for hosting Germany's first-ever elected parliament in 1848-1849.
"A people ready to die for the right to vote is willing to exercise the right to vote," he added to applause.
Anti-government protests broke out at the end of last year in Iran and were suppressed in a January crackdown by security forces, which rights groups say killed tens of thousands.
Pahlavi's voice quivered as he spoke of the relatives of those killed, some of whom were present in the hall.
"You could not have chosen a people who better understand the meaning of the word 'freedom'," he told the foundation.
Pahlavi taking receipt of the prize was not welcomed by all, despite the visible support he enjoyed on the streets of Frankfurt.

Pahlavi's father, Mohammed Reza Pahlavi, was the last shah of Iran, an autocratic ruler who fled into exile in 1979 ahead of a broad revolution that overthrew the monarchy and later became consolidated under Islamist clerical rule.
Others criticise Pahlavi for his vocal support for Israel and what they say is insufficiently distancing himself from his father's autocratic rule.

About 200 prisoners held in Iran signed a letter protesting Pahlavi's receipt of the prize, according to Sahar Sanaie, spokeswoman for the Society for German-Iranians in the state of Hesse, considering him a symbol of a "bygone dictatorship".
The Frankfurt branches of the centre-left SPD and Greens boycotted the event, arguing Pahlavi could not be considered a legitimate representative of the Iranian people.
The Frankfurt branch of the far-left Die Linke said the church should not host the event, pointing to city statutes that prevent the place of worship from hosting political events.
Speaking Saturday, Pahlavi said he was accepting the prize only as a "trustee" until a democratically elected government was in power in Iran.
"I hold it only temporarily," he said. "One day I will place it in the hands of its rightful owners, not on foreign soil but in the capital, Tehran."
28db9fc83e1a5cd8: DOHA: Sistem perbankan dalam talian dan transaksi kewangan negara kekal selamat meskipun terdapat percubaan serangan siber oleh pihak bukan negara, termasuk insiden penggodaman laman web Bank Rakyat baru-baru ini.

Fahmi mengetuai delegasi Malaysia ke Persidangan Plenipotensiari Kesatuan Telekomunikasi Antarabangsa 2026 (ITU PP-26) dari 6 Nov hingga 11 Nov, yang turut menjadi platform penting bagi penglibatan negara dalam perbincangan dan kerjasama antarabangsa berkaitan sektor telekomunikasi serta teknologi digital.

f0b82117346f96a2: PARIS: Gael Monfils, who recently retired from tennis after a 22-year playing career, has been appointed captain of the France Davis Cup team, the French Tennis Federation (FFT) announced Saturday.

1db2ac17e59d2b59: WELLINGTON: New Zealand prime minister Christopher Luxon said Sunday his right-wing coalition had a path back to office, while conceding the vote remained "too close to call" after a hard-fought campaign dominated by cost of living issues.

Neither Luxon's National Party nor the centre-left Labour won enough seats in parliament to form a government without minor parties in an election that put the two main parties neck and neck at 29% – just a few thousand votes separating them.
Preliminary results had National winning the most seats, which would give them a very slim majority if combined with their coalition partners – the populist NZ First and the libertarian ACT.
"National is once again the largest party in parliament, and we have a pathway to forming the next government. But right now it is too close to call," Luxon told supporters in Auckland.
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final votes were tallied on Nov 27.
Those votes – which include those from the tens of thousands of New Zealanders living abroad – could tip the balance of the poll.
"With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations," Luxon said.

At an event with supporters in Upper Hutt, near Wellington, Labour leader Chris Hipkins arrived late to cheers of his nickname "Chippy" – greeted with adulation even as he accepted that his party may not play a role in the next government.
"New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you've said," he told supporters.
"Our next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together, and to find common ground."
Centrist upstart
This week's knife-edge poll drew intense attention to the country's minor parties, in particular the upstart centrist Opportunity Party.
Under the country's mixed-member proportional representation (MMP) system, voters must tick two options – a general party list as well as an individual member to represent their electorate.
Results put Opportunity winning over 5% – the threshold needed to gain seats in parliament without an electorate candidate win, which could give the party a kingmaker role in the next government.
Leader Qiulae Wong has vowed kinder, gentler politics and said she could work with whichever party wins the most seats.
"You guys have voted for unity over division," she said as votes rolled in.
"You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good."
Cost of living
Kiwis are struggling to make ends meet – the price of basic goods remains stubbornly elevated, and unemployment at its highest in more than a decade.
The war in the Middle East and the subsequent global fuel shock have been widely blamed for the hit to New Zealand's economy.

Luxon had hoped his right-wing coalition could cling to power with promises of "no new taxes", after three fractious years in office, two failed bids by his own party to oust him as leader and an economy in the doldrums.
And while National have a path to power and the largest number of seats, they would do so without several of their most senior and highest-performing members.
Deputy leader and finance minister Nicola Willis would not return to parliament due to her party's poor performance in party voting.
And Chris Bishop, the minister for housing, infrastructure and transport, looks set to lose his Hutt South seat, leaving him out of parliament.

f6a76a717d926501: It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters.

At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors.

Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.
