5f6e3d9db66e4bc1: Britain's ambitions for AI, advanced chips, and clean energy rest on mineral supply chains dominated by China, and MPs say they cannot establish whether ministers have a credible plan to reduce that dependence.

The House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee has set ministers ten tests for securing critical minerals. Its verdict is hardly glowing – it cannot be confident the government passes any of them.

The tests cover whether ministers know which industries and technologies need protecting, what minerals they require, where supplies could be disrupted, and how domestic production, overseas partnerships, skills, and financing will close the gaps.

In a report published today, the committee warns that diversifying supplies will take ten to 15 years, and will require sustained investment and cooperation with allies. Completely cutting China out is neither realistic nor desirable, it says. Leaving Beijing with so much leverage is another matter.

Critical minerals underpin everything from batteries and semiconductors to datacenters and military equipment. The designation reflects their economic or security importance and vulnerability to supply disruption, rather than membership of an especially exclusive geological club.

The UK – like pretty much all major industrialized economies including the US, the EU, Japan, and India – is almost entirely dependent on imports of these materials and mineral products. But digging up more ore outside China would solve only part of the problem. The bigger bottleneck is processing.

Citing International Energy Agency figures, the committee says China is the leading refiner for 19 of 20 strategic minerals, with an average market share of 70 percent. A different flag over the mine does not necessarily mean a different route through the refinery.

The exposure extends beyond chips and batteries. As The Register reported in August, erbium is used to amplify signals in fiber-optic links, while yttrium goes into components including ceramic capacitors. IEEE Spectrum warned that China effectively monopolized the processing of both into the industrially usable materials manufacturers need.

That concentration has already caused disruption. China's rare earth export controls in April 2025, introduced following US tariffs, rippled through manufacturing supply chains and forced temporary automotive plant closures. British manufacturers can suffer even when Britain isn't the intended target.

The committee also highlights gallium and germanium, used in advanced semiconductors for radar, communications, and electronic warfare. China accounts for 95 percent and 93 percent of their global production respectively, according to the report [PDF].

Beijing flexing its leverage over chip materials is not new. China announced export licensing requirements for gallium and germanium in July 2023 amid tightening Western restrictions on semiconductor technology.

Yet MPs say the government has not clearly identified which domestic industrial and technological capabilities it wants to protect, making it difficult to determine which supply chains deserve priority.

Nor do import statistics reveal the whole exposure. Minerals can arrive inside batteries, magnets, and other manufactured components, disappearing from view as individual materials. Businesses themselves may not know precisely what lies several layers down their supply chains.

The committee wants confidential mapping and stress-testing with firms in critical sectors, followed by joint purchasing arrangements with allies to give new mining and refining projects dependable customers.

Committee chair Liam Byrne said: "Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy. We cannot re-arm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.

"Yet sixteen years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed. We don't know enough about what minerals we need or where to find them. Our energy costs make processing uneconomic, we're exporting valuable metal waste, and our public finance institutions are shackled by outdated rules."
More than a shopping list

The committee's five-part prescription is to identify the capabilities Britain must protect, map their mineral needs, expand domestic mining, processing, and recycling, pool purchasing power with allies, and establish a dedicated financing facility.
The proposed facility would bring together public funding bodies to back projects through grants, equity, loans, guarantees, and long-term purchase agreements.
"We're never going to eliminate Chinese minerals from our supply chains. But it's foolish to leave Britain exposed to economic coercion when we could be building alternative supplies," Byrne said.
"That's why we need a new Critical Minerals Finance Facility with the financial firepower to invest in new mines, processing plants and recycling, working with our allies to share the costs."

The report argues that existing institutions leave gaps, particularly for early-stage projects. It recommends expanding UK Export Finance's remit and allowing British International Investment to take equity stakes in overseas mineral projects.
Long-term purchasing commitments and price guarantees could help keep strategically important projects commercially viable despite volatile mineral prices.

There is also material closer to home. The report says 80 percent of UK metal products classified as waste are exported. MPs want better sorting and separation infrastructure, alongside more detailed trade data to establish exactly what valuable scrap is leaving the country.
For domestic projects, they recommend designated critical mineral clusters with permitting deadlines, help navigating approvals, energy support, and priority grid access.

Stockpiles could provide a short-term buffer too. The committee calls for an initial reserve covering approximately 60 days of minerals needed for defense capabilities, while stressing that warehouses are no substitute for diversified supply.

None of this offers a quick escape from dependence on China. The committee's argument is that Britain needs to decide what it must protect, work out what those industries actually consume, and help finance alternatives before the next disruption.

"De-risking even a prudent proportion of our supplies will take over a decade. Britain cannot afford to drift," Byrne said. "We must act now before dangerous dependencies become strategic liabilities." ®

f48959b9713d2dd2: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) has put in place regulatory requirements for financial institutions to maintain adequate cybersecurity safeguards, continuously strengthening their defences, said Governor Datuk Seri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour.

This comes as Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim recently warned that Malaysia must remain vigilant against escalating cyber threats amid a series of cyberattacks reported globally that have heightened concerns over the vulnerability of critical digital infrastructure, including the financial sector.
The governor stressed that cybersecurity has always been a priority because it is the foundation of confidence and it could have implications for financial stability.

“We expect financial institutions to adopt a proactive and comprehensive approach to cybersecurity, with strong measures to prevent cyber incidents (as well as) detect and contain threats promptly,” he told Bernama.

Abdul Rasheed said BNM continuously reviews and updates the guidelines, regulations, requirements and standards to ensure that financial institutions remain equipped to address emerging cyber threats.

Incident reporting arrangements and platforms are also in place to enable the central bank and financial institutions to exchange threat intelligence. This helps identify emerging threats early and reduces the risk of contagion across the financial sector.
He noted that BNM’s Risk Management in Technology (RMiT) policy document requires financial institutions to conduct annual “cyber drills”.
These exercises are intended to test banks’ systems, identify weaknesses and ensure they can maintain operational resilience even if their systems are compromised.
He said cybersecurity preparedness must extend across all financial institutions, regardless of their size, as weaknesses in one institution could potentially expose the wider financial system.
“In cybersecurity, the weakest link would affect everyone as entities within the system are all interconnected. Even a small bank could pose a risk to the entire financial system,” he said.

In the event of an attack, the immediate priority would be to contain the threat by isolating affected systems, disconnecting connections where necessary and conducting checks to minimise contagion risk to other systems or institutions.
He said affected institutions might have to temporarily suspend certain online operations while investigations and security assessments are carried out before services could safely resume.
He added that BNM expects financial institutions to recover operations with minimal disruption while safeguarding customer information. — Bernama

0b3108282dcb5b70: The autofill feature of Apple's Safari browser appears to be suffering from a date handling error that occasionally leads it to supply an incorrect credit card expiration date when filling out forms.

The supposed issue has been a sore spot for Apple customers dating back at least to 2017, when the author of an Apple Community forum post complained about changes to the month field in the Autofill credit card expiration date when moving between time zones.

"I've noticed for the last year or so, whenever I travel from Eastern time zone (my home) to Central time zone or even Pacific time zone that my credit card expiration date month changes in Safari Autofill," the Safari user wrote.
Another post in 2021 raised similar concerns.

"I don't know how to reproduce this," the author wrote. "Every few months Safari on any of my devices changes the expiration month of all of my stored credit cards by decreasing the month by 1, for example instead of 10/2029 it changes it to 09/2029."
Three years later, another person posting to Apple's Community forum reported the same issue.

"For a few years now every time I use Autofill on my computer my credit cards (ALL of them) always have their expiration dates change one month earlier," the 2024 post says. "I thought it was just a glitch on my computer but I bought a new computer and didn't transfer anything from my old one and it is still doing it."
An unrelated Autofill bug report from 2024 suggests that if there is an issue, it resides in Apple-owned Safari code rather than Safari's open source WebKit engine.

Wherever the bug may reside, Safari's unreliable handling of credit card dates has kept a complaint-filled Reddit thread going for four years. And the reported month-shifting has been noted in other threads, too.
The Register was unable to reproduce the described behavior, but a reader insists it's still a problem.
"The Safari AutoFill feature sometimes fills in the credit card expiration date wrong," the reader explained. "My credit card expires in December, but sometimes Apple helpfully enters November."
"To be clear, the card is stored correctly when inspected in Settings," our tipster added. "The off-by-one error only happens when filling out a form in Safari, and not consistently."

One possible way this might happen is if the Safari Autofill code implemented the expiration date using Swift's DateComponent type and stored it as a Calendar object with UTC as the TimeZone identifier. Doing so would anchor the date to a specific time. If the date components were extracted in Pacific Time, the value would be represented as eight hours ahead (PST). So 9/1/2027 at 00:00 would appear as 8/31/2027 at 16:00.

Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but we're told Apple's Help Desk – or "Helpless Desk" as our source put it – advised clearing the browser cache and re-entering details of the affected credit card.
If that works, it suggests Safari's handling of cached data in the context of Autofill dates may need to be revisited.
Apple does not maintain a public bug database and the community-maintained OpenRadar sheds no light on these reports. ®

70838a2d72ac3386: Welcome to Friday and therefore to a fresh edition of On Call, The Register's weekly tale of tech support trials and tribulations that readers kindly share.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Mason," who told us he once worked at a hospital doing tech support for its research labs.
"One of the labs was for a doctor who was one of the world's top organ transplant researchers" Mason told On Call.
The doctor was also a voracious consumer of – ahem – adult entertainment, a habit that saw his PC and other machines around the lab often come down with a nasty case of malware.
Mason got to clean that up, sometimes multiple times in a single week.
The doctor's foibles were widely known around the hospital, as was the fact that his activities violated several workplace policies.
Mason pointed this out to his boss every time he cleaned up a fresh malware outbreak but such was the doctor's status that management never intervened.

And then the hospital was hit by a nasty cyber-worm that did a lot of damage. During the cleanup, Mason's colleagues found logs that showed the doctor's PC was the source of the infection, and that he had been indulging in his online hobby at the time the worm arrived.
Mason assumed this would be the moment at which the doctor would finally be held accountable and face disciplinary action.

Instead the doctor made a bargain with the IT department to henceforth use only a designated PC when pursuing – ahem – personal and/or intimate matters. And he would only use office PCs for actual work.
The hospital's tech team rescued a PC from its e-waste pile for this job.
"Get this thing going and deliver it to Doctor Pervert," Mason's boss ordered.

By this stage, Mason had had enough. He escalated his protests, telling his boss that indulging this doctor was unprofessional, likely exposed the hospital to lawsuits, wasted IT department resources, and was just wrong.
"What do you want to hear?" his boss replied. "The CIO told me do this or get another job."
After Mason prepped that PC, he only needed to clean up malware about once a year – after the poor machine was so overrun with malware that it no longer served the doctor's purposes.
Mason left the hospital while this PC was still in place.

"You'll be shocked, no doubt, to learn that years later the doctor's graduate students filed a lawsuit," he told On Call. "And that the separate fun-time computer was one of the pieces of evidence that the hospital knew about his – ahem – proclivities and not just ignored them but facilitated them."

Have you been asked to cover up revolting behavior? Or ignore policy? Click here to share your story with On Call. It's our policy to tell a great tech support story week, so we appreciate every contribution. ®

56791ba0ab009ead: Machado returns to a hopeful, cautious nation
Originally published on Global Voices
María Corina Machado arriving in Caracas after months of hiding and exile. Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Thousands of people took to the Valle-Coche highway in Caracas to welcome the opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela after 16 months in hiding and ten months in exile. The massive gathering was one of celebration, but her compatriots were also filled with doubts about what comes next.

After more than a year in the shadows, forced into hiding following her kidnapping — allegedly by government paramilitaries — at her last public protest in 2025, Machado quietly slipped out of the country. She emerged on the global stage later that year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize honoring her social organization campaign during Venezuela’s 2024 presidential elections, which were ultimately stolen by Nicolás Maduro. Since the former Venezuelan president’s capture on January 3, 2026, Machado has tried — and failed — to enter the country on at least seven occasions, claiming that the administration established by U.S. President Donald Trump didn’t allow her in.

On the morning of October 25, however, Machado was spotted in the city of Barquisimeto, where she visited the Santa Rosa church, and at about 10:25 that evening, her caravan passed through Santa Mónica, along the main route that leads to Venezuela’s captital:
Estoy aquí. Con ustedes
— María Corina Machado (@MariaCorinaYA) October 25, 2026
I am here. With you all.

Drivers excitedly honked their horns; in a crowd of about 3,000, people shouted slogans. Starting from the state of Lara, Machado’s caravan crossed Yaracuy, Carabobo, and Aragua as it inched toward Caracas — a journey of more than 300 kilometres that took her nearly 11 hours to complete.
A different country

On the heels of the January 3 United States military operation that captured Nicolás Maduro, whose 2024 re-election was questioned both inside and outside of Venezuela, then vice president Delcy Rodríguez took over as interim president.

Since August, her interim government has been negotiating with Dinorah Figuera, president of the National Assembly who was elected in 2015, in a Washington-driven dialogue process. Despite having promoted participation in the 2024 presidential elections, Machado’s party, Vente Venezuela, has had no representation in those negotiations.
The crowd waited for hours for Maria Corina Machado's arrival to the capital city. Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Yet, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio attributed Machado’s safe return to those talks, which he claimed had already allowed for the release of hundreds of political prisoners and the return of hundreds of exiled opposition figures. Rubio called on all political actors to back them because they represent “the best opportunity Venezuela has had in thirty years.”

Faced with political demobilization, Venezuelans are used to seeing protests where the majority of participants are activists, leaders, and members of civil society organizations — people who are well-informed because it is their job to be — but Machado’s gathering was different. There were people without party shirts or hats; just a combination of families, friends, and civilians who seemed motivated by her return and hopeful for their country.

People began to assemble on the highway around 3:00 p.m. local time. After hours of waiting, the gathering turned into a party — the type of celebration that many did not dare to have after January 3.

Machado barely spoke; she did not have a megaphone and was in the tray of a pickup truck with a security detail around her. She gave no statements to the media during the caravan; instead, she listened to and greeted the crowd, hugging people, touching their hands, and letting herself be seen. On this occasion, people did not go to hear proposals, but simply to see her.

At one point, two patrols from the Directorate General of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) passed by. The people closest to the highway lane began shouting at them, “Get out, get out!” but no one blocked their path or touched their doors or windows and the patrols continued on their way. Known as Venezuela’s political police, the DGCIM was one of the bodies singled out for 2024’s repressive post-election measures, in which more than 2,300 people were detained.
New uncertainties

Asked about the possible aftermaths of Machado’s return, caravan participants shared differing perspectives. Veterinarian Marianna Torres had no doubts about the order of things: Venezuela must have presidential elections, and soon, but not with the same electoral institutions that have permitted electoral fraud in the past. For her, all branches of power are corrupt and must be cleaned up before any election.

She also urged people looking at Venezuela from the outside to stop listening solely to politicians and pay attention to what “everyday Venezuelans” — the ones who know there are still political prisoners, human rights violations, and government authoritarian control — are saying.

Gabriela Santander, a publicist and activist for the Encuentro Ciudadano party, thought almost the opposite regarding the timeline. Stressing that she had been waiting for this day for months, since before Machado left, she believes that going to vote now, without an independent electoral arbiter or an impartial Supreme Tribunal of Justice (TSJ), would be falling into a trap. Her deadline is concrete: if a new Electoral National Center is not in place by the end of the first quarter of 2027, the time to put on pressure will arrive.

Santander suspects that behind Machado’s return — which she believes could not have happened without Washington's approval — are agreements that no one has disclosed, especially since Rubio confirmed that his government had negotiated her return with the interim government “many weeks ago.” What Santander noticed the night of the caravan, however, was something more important: people had been on the highway for more than four hours and authorities had not tried to detain them.

Attorney Joyffer Briceño took a pragmatic view of the situation. While he sees Machado as the leader of those who want to restore the country’s institutions, he does not mistake emotion for change. “Those who hold power today are the same ones who were part of the crisis for years,” he explained. “I want something less abstract than an economic growth figure; I want the improvement to be felt in the pockets of every Venezuelan.”

For José Gregorio Rodríguez Cham, Machado’s arrival carries a different weight. His father, Julio Rodríguez Salazar, is a political prisoner, so he attended the event with other relatives to continue demanding the release of the 322 political prisoners who, according to Foro Penal, remain detained. He believes that new elections would be different because of the oversight of the United States, but he does not deny that the repressive apparatus in Venezuela remains intact, and that dismantling it will take time. What he years for in the coming months are elections and freedom, starting with that of his family.
Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Raquel Bugallo, a merchant in Caracas, remains somewhat suspicious of outside help. She believes that the international humanitarian aid Venezuela expected was overshadowed by economic interests, and that oil has been both Venezuela’s greatest wealth and “worst curse.” While she didn’t reject Rubio's call for understanding among all sectors, she did attach a condition: finding common ground, as long as the country can move forward. Her message to the international community was the shortest of the night: “If you are not going to help us, don’t get in our way.”

The day after Machado’s return, Delcy Rodríguez quipped that “the show could have been avoided.” Meanwhile, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights reminded the Venezuelan state of its obligation to guarantee the life, integrity, and political rights of the leader. Between November 11 and 15, the dialogue table will meet again, for the first time with Machado inside the country.

In the meantime, Venezuelans can savour the feeling of having spent hours on the streets without that familiar fear of repression. While repressive bodies were still present, passing in patrols through the crowd, on October 25, 2026, with Machado waving from the back of a pickup truck, the people stared back at them and told them to go, which must have felt something like progress.
Written by Óscar Calles
c5e48eab8233c409: SINGAPORE: Singapore Airlines, long a benchmark for premium travel, is spending more than S$2 billion (US$1.6 billion) to upgrade long-haul seats and provide larger double-bed suites to compete with rivals that are pouring money into high-end cabins.
The airline on Friday unveiled new cabins in all four travel classes in the biggest and most comprehensive overhaul in its history, with the new seats due from the second half of 2027.

In first class, centre seats convert into what Singapore Airlines calls the largest double bed in commercial aviation. Business class gets sliding privacy doors for the first time on the airline, alongside a fully flat bed.

The launch comes as carriers globally such as Air France, British Airways and United Airlines pour billions into premium travel despite industry-wide delays in production and certification of new seats.
Surging fuel costs have squeezed margins and pushed up fares, deterring some more cost-conscious economy passengers, although premium travel has remained relatively resilient.

The investment "underpins our long-standing commitment to continually raise the bar of premium air travel," Yeoh Phee Teik, Singapore Airlines' senior vice-president customer experience, said at a briefing on Wednesday.
The Singapore Airlines programme covers 72 aircraft, a mix of Airbus A350-900s being retrofitted and Boeing 777-9 jets on order that together will comprise the majority of its long-haul fleet.
The cabins were originally designed for the 777-9, which is expected to become Singapore Airlines' new long-haul flagship as the A380, which offers smaller double beds, eventually retires.
But the 777-9's entry into service has slipped for years, which Singapore Airlines chief commercial officer Lee Lik Hsin told Reuters had led the carrier to widen the programme to its A350s.

He said the S$2 billion-plus investment included a S$1.1 billion A350 refurbishment plan announced in 2024 and was funded from the airline's strong cash balance, which stood at S$9.1 billion as of end-June.

Most of the investment goes to premium cabins because business and first-class seats cost far more per unit than economy seats, Lee said, with the carrier setting no spending ceiling and planning to keep investing when appropriate to maintain its market leadership.
"Our competitive advantage doesn't derive from aircraft cabin product alone," he said. "It is the hard product, the soft service, the operational excellence. And...it is our people."

David Flynn, editor-in-chief of industry publication Executive Traveller, said the new first class with a unique curved cabin design that borrowed space from the aisles to add personal space to each suite ranked among the world's best.

"Business class represent a solid and much-needed catch up to the competition, rather than a mighty leap ahead," he said. "It's hard to top Qatar's business class Qsuite, let alone the next-gen version coming in 2027, but in features and usability, Singapore Airlines looks to have Emirates and arguably Cathay beat here."
Delays and certification

The unveiling arrives against a backdrop of persistent delays. Boeing first targeted 777-9 deliveries around 2020 but repeated certification setbacks, engine issues, the pandemic and tighter oversight by the US Federal Aviation Administration have pushed that to 2027, with Lufthansa expected to be the launch operator.
Lee said slippage on its A350 refurbishment plan and the 777-9 seating were both driven by certification issues.
"The seats are certified on the 777-9, but the 777-9 aeroplane itself is not certified, and the seats have not yet been certified on the A350," he said.
The A350 certification delay had pushed back their introduction by about half a year, he added.
As airlines design more premium offerings with bespoke features that regulators need to ensure meet stringent crash-safety standards, seat certification has become a bottleneck across the industry.
Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg last week told investors that deliveries of its 787 Dreamliners had been affected by seat certification challenges.
6975dd1c12be3208: HONG KONG, Nov 6 — Asian tech firms suffered a bloodbath today as investors tracked a collapse on Wall Street fuelled by fears that Democrats will ramp up regulations of the AI industry following their blowout victory in this week’s US midterm elections.

Trading boards were a sea of red in early business, with Seoul and Tokyo taking the brunt of the selling as traders fled to the hills amid uncertainty about a sector that had pushed stock markets to record highs just five months ago.

While the historic “blue wave” in Tuesday’s vote had been initially welcomed on hopes it could put pressure on President Donald Trump to wind down his war against Iran, fears about the impact on the AI buildout soon came to the fore.
Data centres have faced broad opposition from US voters across the political spectrum, and many midterm winners have pledged to put the brakes on such projects.
Analysts said investors were also spooked by a call from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders for a national moratorium on their building.

The results compounded already heightened fears about the hundreds of billions firms had pumped into the sector and when they would see a return, while the recent spike in borrowing costs also fuelled concerns about their financial position.
The eye-watering rally in many companies’ valuations had also caused unease on trading floors.

Michael Hewson at MCH Market Insights said investors were selling up because of “concerns that we might see greater opposition to AI buildout plans, with the results in Texas prompting concerns that politicians in the state might target Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX due to his support for Trump”.

New York’s Nasdaq plunged 5.5 per cent in its worst day—perentage-wise—since April last year when Trump unveiled his wide-ranging global tariffs. The S&P 500 tanked more than four percent and the Dow more than three percent.
Bloomberg said the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had collapsed around 16 per cent this week, putting it on course for its worst run since April last year.

Trump blamed the collapse on the Democrats, writing on Truth Social: “The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday - So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”
The heavy selling continued in Asia.
Seoul plunged almost nine per cent at one point, with chip giant SK hynix off 10 per cent while rival Samsung was eight per cent down.
The Kospi more than doubled between the end of December and mid-June, when it hit a record, and has since then lost almost 50 per cent.
Tokyo dived seven per cent as Kioxia and SoftBank gave back more than 10 per cent, with Advantest more than eight percent lower.
TSMC’s seven-per cent drop dragged Taipei’s Taiex around eight per cent lower.
Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney and Singapore were all down more than one per cent, with Wellington and Manila also in the red.
“The blood is in the streets, folks,” said Neil Wilson at Saxo Markets.

“The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh data centre buildout... this looks totally overdone but the nature of sell-everything of this market means we need to look for some stability first.”
The mood was also dampened by a fresh lift in oil prices, extending Thursday’s gains after plunging on the midterm results amid hopes for an end to the Iran war.
Traders were keeping eyes on developments in the crisis after US and Iranian leaders had indicated progress earlier in the week.
US jobs data is also due later in the day, following broadly positive readings earlier in the week. — AFP
0b111785b94a26d1: British comedian and actor Russell Brand has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, related to multiple victims, after a four-week trial in London. He was acquitted on three other charges. The offences for which Brand was convicted occurred nearly two decades ago. Meanwhile, United Kingdom police are investigating further allegations of rape made by two other women. For the six women who came forward to report their experiences, the verdict marks the culmination of a long and undoubtedly difficult journey through the criminal legal system. Much of the public attention will now likely turn to Brand himself: his sentence, his public reputation and whether he will seek to appeal. But we should also be asking what this verdict means for victim-survivors of sexual violence. Sexual violence is common but justice is rare Though the Brand case occurred in the UK, the rates of sexual violence and trends in justice outcomes are very similar there as they are in Australia. Unfortunately, when we examine those trends, we see justice in response to sexual violence is incredibly rare. In Australia, one in five women has experienced sexual assault since the age of 15. Yet only about 8% report it to police. Of these, very few proceed to court. Of those who do report, about one in four do so in the first year after the assault. For most, however, it takes several years before reporting to police. Often this is because of: shame or embarrassment a feeling police won’t be able to do anything fearing they won’t be believed fearing repercussions from the perpetrator. For the few who do have their day in court, it is widely recognised that legal processes can cause further harm, or a “second violence” which can exacerbate trauma through: legal processes of repeatedly providing accounts of what occurred intense cross-examination a lack of dignity. Justice remains rare, yet is it really justice when the legal process is itself so often the source of further harm to victim-survivors? Consent is active, specific and can be withdrawn any time One of the wider and more positive implications of the Brand verdict is it reinforces some fundamental principles of sexual consent. In Australia, and similarly in the UK, consent means active and free agreement. Consent can be given for some acts and not others, and it can be withdrawn at any time – including during an otherwise consensual sexual encounter. This was a clear takeaway from the Brand conviction. In one instance, the victim-survivor had initially agreed to sexual activity with him, but described how he subsequently violated her boundaries and continued despite her asking him to stop. The jury’s verdict affirms a person’s right to determine what sexual activity they want to engage in, and their right to withdraw consent at any time. Yet, persistent attitudes and “rape myths” surrounding men’s sexual entitlement have long undermined these core principles of consent. Often it is victim-survivors who are blamed. Celebrity and social power can further reinforce such dynamics, particularly where influential men are surrounded by institutions and peers willing to excuse or minimise harmful behaviour. Fame and status should never diminish anyone’s right to bodily autonomy. Perpetrator accountability is vital For survivors of sexual violence, a guilty verdict can offer a profoundly important form of justice: recognition that a wrong has been committed and the person responsible is held accountable. Yet we should perhaps be cautious about assuming a criminal conviction, and incarceration of the perpetrator, will always bring closure and healing for survivors. The consequences of sexual violence can persist long after criminal proceedings conclude. Survivors may continue to experience the emotional, relational and practical impacts of their experiences, including the additional distress associated with pursuing justice. And it is important to recognise the absence of a guilty verdict does not mean the absence of any harm. Accountability takes many forms. Some victim-survivors seek criminal accountability of the perpetrator, while others may seek recognition through other means, including restorative justice processes. Perpetrator accountability can also take the form of apology and a commitment to positive change. Unfortunately, this form of accountability is rarely seen. More needs to change Brand’s conviction is arguably a significant moment of accountability and recognition. For many victim-survivors watching, it may offer some reassurance that even powerful men can be held accountable for their use of violence. But it is important to recognise that one high-profile conviction cannot undo the injustice many survivors experience. We need justice systems that are more accessible and trauma-responsive, as well as institutions that are willing to confront sexual violence. We need wider community change to ensure sexual violence is taken seriously, and that survivors are not blamed and shamed for another person’s use of harm. And we need greater emphasis on genuine perpetrator accountability, through recognition of harm caused and a commitment to change. The women involved in this case have been deservedly praised for their courage. It is no small burden they have carried to seek justice. Ultimately, though, we should be working towards legal systems and a society where survivors do not have to demonstrate extraordinary courage simply to be heard and supported. The National Sexual Assault, Family and Domestic Violence Counselling Line – 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732) – is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week for any Australian who has experienced, or is at risk of, family and domestic violence and/or sexual assault. Anastasia Powell teaches family violence specialist casework in the Graduate Certificate in Domestic & Family Violence at RMIT University. Anastasia receives funding from the Australian Research Council, is a director of Our Watch (Australia's national organisation for the prevention of violence against women), and works in direct practice with survivors of sexual violence. She is the author of the book 'The Aftermath of Trauma' (Palgrave, 2026) and host of the podcast 'Trauma & Transformation'.
e8800235b886483c: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 6 — Silicon Valley bosses who spent two years cozying up to US President Donald Trump now face a Democratic Congress already threatening subpoenas, after midterm elections in which antipathy toward artificial intelligence swayed voters.
“AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath,” Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said on Tuesday.
Senator Ed Markey, for his part, warned tech executives they would need to “plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”

It is a cold shower for tech bosses who rallied behind Trump after his 2024 win, with Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and others front and center at his January 2025 inauguration.

Musk went furthest, spending more than US$250 million to help elect Trump and then taking charge of his DOGE cost-cutting drive. He poured nearly half a billion dollars more into backing Republicans in the midterms.
Once they take control of both chambers on January 3, Democrats will control the committees that can compel an executive to testify or hand over internal documents under threat of prosecution.
In 2020, the heads of Amazon, Apple, Facebook and Google were called to answer for their market dominance.
Musk, OpenAI’s Sam Altman or Nvidia’s Jensen Huang—one of Trump’s closest advisers on AI—could now face the same ordeal.
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, elected senator for Michigan despite more than US$5 million spent against him by America PAC, the political committee funded by Musk, wants to go further.
He is calling for a “full-on pause” in the development of the most powerful AI systems and a US-China treaty to “pause and ban superintelligence,” meaning AI that would surpass human intelligence.
To pass legislation, however, lawmakers will need to rally a party divided on the issue and overcome the veto of Trump, who remains president until January 2029.
No major tech boss had commented on the election as of yesterday except Musk, who joked: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”
Parts of the industry had begun distancing themselves from Republicans before the vote.

The main pro-AI political fund, financed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz—one of whose cofounders backed Trump in 2024 — received no new donations from April through the end of September, as public distrust of AI grew.
Meta has hired former Democratic staffers in recent months to represent it in Congress, according to Axios.
Shapeshifters
Criticism is also coming from the Republican side.
“Voters are primed to reward whichever political party delivers on holding Big Tech accountable,” Daniel Cochrane, a senior fellow at the conservative Institute for Family Studies, told AFP.
“In this election, concerns about AI’s social and economic impacts shifted votes,” he said, pointing to data centers as well as AI’s effects on jobs and children.
According to an NBC News exit poll, AI and data centers were “a crucial or a major factor” for 56 percent of voters in their choice for Congress.
“Let’s not confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate,” said Adam Kovacevich, CEO of Chamber of Progress, an influential centrist coalition funded by major tech companies.

“There’s only one thing that sinks the US economy, it’s the AI trade,” and “the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers,” Chamath Palihapitiya warned during an election-night livestream of the All-In podcast, which he co-hosts with other prominent pro-Trump Silicon Valley investors.
Even market analyst Dan Ives, known for his bullish outlook on tech growth, now estimates that 10 percent of the 800 to 1,000 new data centers planned in the United States “will not happen.”
“The tech bros are shapeshifters,” said Cochrane, who expects Zuckerberg “to have another mea culpa” before an “aggressive Dem congress.”
“Ultimately, the tech bros are for the tech bros,” he said. — AFP
16ade08f04c7d18d: Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community

Since October 27, at least 20 online media outlets and social media accounts in Albania have been waging a coordinated attack against the staff of fact-checking media service Faktoje Center, based in Tirana. A partner of Global Voices, Faktoje has been promoting accountability based on the right to information and transparency since 2018.

Faktoje and its team members, in particular its director, Klodiana Kapo, are facing a series of coordinated attacks from media outlets that have been circulating and reproducing articles that question Faktoje’s funding, financial management and independence, using its publicly available financial statements to cast doubt on the organisation’s credibility.

Faktoje is a certified signatory of the Code of Principles of the International Fact-Finding Network and the Code of Standards of the European Fact-Checking Standards Network. Both require high levels of public transparency in disclosing sources of funding and methodologies of work. This coordinated campaign aims to undermine the impact of Faktoje’s important work by maliciously using financial information that the organization voluntarily publishes, but stripping it of context and mischaracterizing its influence.

Faktoje considers these attacks to be directly connected to its fact-checking activities under its partnership with Meta, in the context of its recent fact-checking work covering the ongoing protests and debunking misleading narratives targeting protesters.

Since its inception eight years ago, Faktoje has stood at the forefront of the fight for freedom of expression, independent journalism, and information integrity in Albania and the wider Balkans region, including participation in the regional Western Balkans Anti-Disinformation Hub, the Anti-Disinformation Network for the Balkans and the continent-wide European Digital Media Observatory – EDMO Network.

Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community. Albanian authorities and European institutions need to speak up publicly for independent fact-checkers and journalists, and to ensure their safety, while media outlets reporting on civil society funding need to do so accurately and in context.

Global Voices joins the European Fact-Checking Standards Network and the International Fact-Checking Network in vehemently condemning those attacks on our partner. We stand in solidarity with our colleagues.
4e7f81c4ff53615b: It appears that the dust has settled, at least for now as the judicial process takes over, on the Tabung Haji (TH) “mismanagement” issue.
It was widely commented upon following the release of the full royal commission of inquiry (RCI) report just before a state election.
There were allegations of embezzlement (sakau) and unadulterated corruption at this investment institution.
Presumably the intention was to throw dirt on the past administration.
Mind you the full RCI report had been on the back burner for almost three years before its release.

Some say, tactically speaking as in urban guerrilla political warfare, it was kept under wraps for an opportune time such that its release could inflict the highest degree of damage to the political opposition.
Sadly, that was not to be as the state election results stand testimony.
To add a degree of altruistic intent, the reason offered was that it could not be released earlier as the flagship, TH, was being given time to keep its policies and practices in order.

It was vehemently argued that releasing the RCI findings earlier might have affected TH’s credibility as an institution set up specifically to enable investors to finance their trips to the holy land (through consistent savings).

Worse still, it was rationalised that its depositors, largely from the country’s heartland, may have withdrawn their deposits en masse. This desperate action would have resulted in financial chaos with spillover effects on other financial institutions in the country.
To the naïve, uninformed and politically ignorant, this justification had a degree of credence.

A lawmaker had highlighted possible offences (crimes which include financial deception, falsification of accounting records, the unlawful distribution of ‘hibah’ dividends), as the Tabung Haji Act 1995 forbids declaring or paying profits when liabilities exceed assets.

To top it off, as a safe measure, criminal breach of trust is included. That is indeed a mouthful but then politicians are known for rhetoric, most times self-serving, and in certain instances illogical.

To date two ex-ministers have been charged. At the crux is the Attorney-General’s Chambers’s decision to charge the ex-CEO and ex-chief financial officer with “misleading the board” under Section 417 of the Penal Code.
The legal system only looks at the charge and decides on guilt or innocence. The reasons for such a criminal act, altruistic or not, are inconsequential.

In TH’s case it is common knowledge that the beneficiaries of this “misleading” were the investors who were paid handsome dividends. This state of affairs should not have been so as the provisions of an Act were breached.

It is obvious that the persons involved at TH accrued no gains. It is neither embezzlement nor corruption — if so, the charges would be completely different and fall under the MACC Act 2009 or Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001.
Nonetheless, this episode was milked for what it is worth to cast aspersions reflecting on the integrity and level of corruption of the government of the day.

The inquiry examined TH’s management and operations between 2014 and 2020. It concluded that the combination of high hibah commitments, governance weaknesses and accounting shortcomings affected its long-term financial sustainability.

For context, the RCI found that pressure to maintain high hibah payouts contributed to the deterioration of the fund’s financial position and pushed it towards riskier investment decisions. Unfortunately, these led to certain investments turning sour.

In its report, the RCI said LTH continued declaring attractive hibah between 2014 and 2017 despite its weakening financial position, presumably increasing pressure on management to generate higher returns.
“The attractive returns encouraged more deposits from savers, increasing TH’s financial obligations while creating expectations that similar levels of hibah would continue”.

It is obvious here who benefitted from the higher returns – the investors. Surely there is a moral justification here as the interests of the investors was paramount – Where is the “sakau”, or embezzlement as alleged by certain quarters.
How it was done, through revaluations of assets or flouting global accounting standards and whether or not there was criminal intent, is left for the courts to decide.
This expectation on higher investment returns cannot be denied. An element of greed entered the equation and no one questioned it, notwithstanding the audited accounts.
By law, no crime can be justified by the circumstances leading to it or supporting it within the ecosystem.

In an unrelated incident to provide perspective, on Nov 2, a 43-year-old unemployed father of five was sentenced to six months’ jail for stealing RM394 worth of baby formula and groceries from a supermarket in Kelantan.
It was commented that an accused’s financial hardship and family responsibilities did not automatically warrant a lighter sentence.
A proverb from the Tirukkural, an ancient Tamil literary work written by philosopher Tiruvalluvar, was quoted by the magistrate.
This only reinforces the point that the reason is inconsequential, heart breaking as it is.

In the case of TH, where is the moral ground? The investors received dividends which they were not entitled to as the Act specifically provides the stipulation on the relationship between the assets and liabilities before dividends can be declared.

In brief, investors have no good title to the dividends as it was a result of a criminal act purportedly committed by the ex-CEO and ex-CFO in misleading the board – who themselves are held to account on their fiduciary duties (healthy, professional scepticism).
This has resulted in a burden to the government in relation to the special purpose vehicle created to prevent the pilgrim fund from insolvency (circa RM10 billion).

Who will take the high road to return the dividends for the affected years. Now that TH is in a healthy state perhaps future dividends should be channelled not to the investors but to fund the special purpose vehicle.
This is food for thought in the years where “sakau” is being freely thrown about to show fellow politicians in a bad light — just to score points.
The word “sakau” has deep negative connotations. It should be used judiciously and not crowed about at any half opportunity. This action is in itself unethical
As the man fed his hungry children, does the end justify the means? Do we need to keep investors happy or is there more to it – what are their obligations?
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

5bcccb25572c860b: Iranians at a pro-regime rally in Tehran's Enqelab Square on Nov. 4, 2026, taunt U.S. President Donald Trump and his deputy, JD Vance. Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty ImagesWhile votes were still being counted in the U.S. midterm elections, administration figures in Washington were already inviting speculation over how the results might be connected to the conflict with Iran. On the morning after the election, Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that the major reason for the dramatic loss for Republicans was the American public’s opposition to the war. “Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” he wrote, in reference to the ongoing conflict that began with U.S.-Israeli airstrikes against Iran in late February 2026. While it is rare for a vice president to make such a critical proclamation about their own administration’s policy, President Donald Trump later stated that he did not disagree with Vance’s appraisal of the role that frustration with the Iran war played in voters’ minds. But whether this changes Trump’s view on next steps in the ongoing conflict remains unclear. Reporting over the past few weeks has indicated that the U.S. military has been actively preparing options and increasing capabilities in the Persian Gulf region in the event the president directs a resumption of hostilities. As an expert on Middle East affairs and a former senior official at the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, I’m aware that months of conflict have failed to bring Iran to its knees, force regime change or militarily defeat a perceived threat to U.S. assets and allies. Escalating now is unlikely to change those realities – and it carries the additional risk of further damaging Republicans in the eyes of Americans voters as they turn toward the 2028 presidential race. Even if Trump were to ratchet up the conflict, moreover, it’s unclear how much wiggle room he’ll have come January facing a Democratic Congress almost uniformly opposed to the war. Demonstrators protest the Iran war near the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Nov. 2, 2026. Kevin Carter/Getty Images Sunk costs Part of the issue facing Iran war hawks in Washington now is that the conflict has caused serious setbacks for the regime in Tehran without satisfying the officially stated strategic reasons for going to war. They argue that pulling back now – as welcome as that might be for Americans struggling with the associated rising cost of fuel – may allow Iran to rebuild before the conflict is “won.” Moreover, it would render the military and reputational costs already sunk by Washington as wasted. Among the achievements of this war touted by the Trump administration has been the death of former Supreme Leader Ali Khameini, along with the killing of scores of senior leaders within the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps – including individuals like the former head of Iran’s National Security Council Ali Larijani. Significant elements of Iran’s air defense and radar network, ballistic missile and drone production, and storage and launch sites have also been destroyed. And Iran’s already outdated navy and air force has been further degraded. Meanwhile, the U.S.-imposed naval blockade against Iranian-linked shipping in the Persian Gulf cut off a crucial lifeline for Iran’s economy. And additional sanctions and economic penalties imposed by Washington have served to further devalue Iran’s currency and deprive Iran of additional financial links to the international banking system. Down but not out Yet for all the U.S. successes in degrading the Iranian military by limitless aerial bombardment and the significant financial pressure against the Iranian economy, an obvious endgame remains elusive. Despite weakening the Iranian government – now led by Ali Khameinei’s son, Mojtaba, and a new echelon of senior IRGC commanders – the Islamic Republic remains intact. Moreover, it still possesses enough ballistic missiles and drones to hold the region at risk, while continuing to impose significant control over its population. Meanwhile, U.S. military spending continues to rise. In September, the U.S. Congressional Budget Office assessed that the military costs of the Iran War had already totaled US$38 billion. Since then, that number has only increased. And that is to say nothing of the associated global economic costs that have resulted from Iran’s de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz – a key shipping route for oil and gas. Should Trump decide to change course on Iran, he – and others – may think that the money, effort and lives of 19 American servicemen killed in the conflict would have been spent with no obvious objective achieved. Yet continued military expenditure with no strategic endgame could only magnify those same costs. The casket of Army Sgt. Angel Rampersad – one of 19 U.S. service members killed in the Iran war. Spencer Platt/Getty Images To Iran, the midterm results have not changed its public position. Mojtaba Khameini has issued statements directing the IRGC to widen the conflict in the region and perhaps beyond should the U.S. and Israel attack again. At the same time, a statement attributed to him indicates that hostilities between the United States and Iran will persist regardless of the balance of party political power in Washington. This raises questions about the prospects for diplomacy. During the summer, the U.S. and Iran agreed to an initial 14-point memorandum of understanding that, if finalized, could have brought a permanent end to the hostilities. But since the 60-day clock on that agreement lapsed, no parallel diplomatic agreement has emerged. No practical solution Even with the major shift in the U.S. political landscape, it remains unclear whether Trump will resume operations against Iran before the new Congress is sworn in. The messy election result in Israel – which has left the pro-war, and potentially outgoing, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyanu with potentially more reason to double-down in Iran – only complicates matters. The U.S. military certainly appears to be ready to engage in a new round of attacks against Iran if so directed, and Iran is ready to retaliate. But given the shortcomings in the U.S. inventory – with munitions and missile and air defense capabilities depleted by eight months of war – escalation is something Trump and his inner circle will have to consider with caution. Iran might force the issue by engaging in asymmetric attacks in the region or beyond that they have not attempted already. Or it could launch a coordinated offensive with its partners in the region – notably the Houthis in Yemen, who have become more active in their own conflict with Saudi Arabia in recent months. But save an event that the Trump administration perceives is giving it cover to act, there are no clear indications emerging from Washington as to which way it will move. Vance diagnosed a widely perceived political problem for Republicans: Voters don’t want more war. But what he noticeably didn’t mention was a practical solution. The Middle East conflict – and the United States’ role in it – are, as such, locked in a stalemate. America and Iran have both borne significant political, military and economic costs. A decision not to pursue an endgame would leave those sunk; doing so may only increase them. d773c67d102d324d: Chris Hyde/Getty ImagesThe Rugby League World Cup (RLWC) reaches its semi-finals this weekend, in a tournament that’s been marked by upsets, nail-biting finishes and some lopsided scorelines. On Saturday in Newcastle, New Zealand’s Kiwi Ferns face Fetu Samoa in the women’s competition, before the Kiwis take on an unbeaten Tonga. Sunday’s matches in Sydney see Australia’s Jillaroos meet Fiji, while their counterparts the Kangaroos face Samoa in a rematch of the previous RLWC men’s final. Pacific nations feature in all four semi-finals. But while the teams represent countries across the region, the vast majority of their players were born in Australia or New Zealand. Our analysis of the semi-final squads found 85% of the women and 95% of the men were born in these two countries. Many have also represented other nations during their international careers. These figures speak to the tight connections between Pacific countries, Australia and New Zealand – and the opportunities rugby league offers players with ties to more than one nation. Small populations, big ties By comparing squad profiles with population data, we can see how migration, family connections and population trends are reflected on the rugby league field. Population size is no guarantee of success in international rugby league. England and France, with populations of around 59 million and 66 million respectively, have already been eliminated. Yet Tonga, home to just 105,000 people, has reached the men’s semi-finals. The Cook Islands, with fewer than 15,000 residents, is the smallest country represented at the tournament. Although the Cook Islands is not in the semi-finals, seven players across the remaining squads have previously represented this proud nation, including Kiwi stars Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad and Apii Nicholls. Generations of migration across Te Moana Nui a Kiwa (the Pacific Ocean) and the Tasman Sea have created deep family ties between these countries. In the women’s semi-finals, 57% of players were born in Australia and another 28% in New Zealand. Twelve players across the Kiwi Ferns and Samoa squads have previously represented other countries, highlighting the overlapping national ties within Pacific rugby league. The Australia-Fiji semi-final, meanwhile, presents a different picture. Only one Jillaroos player in the final team list, Tiana Penitani Gray, has previously represented another country (Tonga), while none of Fiji’s players have done so. Club affiliations show a similar concentration in Australia: 86% of players across the four women’s semi-final squads compete in the National Rugby League Women’s Premiership (NRLW). They are based mostly with Australian clubs, though seven play with New Zealand’s Warriors Women. Fiji is the only team to draw heavily on players from outside the competition. A younger Pacific In the men’s semi-finals, 95% of players were born in Australia (50%) or New Zealand (45%). Seventeen players in the NZ-Tonga squads have previously represented another country, while just two players across the four men’s semi-final teams compete outside the National Rugby League (NRL). The strong presence of NRL and NRLW players also highlights the sporting opportunities available in Australia and New Zealand, and the increasingly diverse populations of both countries. We see such trends in wider migration patterns. In 2023, Australia and New Zealand recorded net migration gains, while Tonga, Samoa and Fiji experienced net losses. Another notable demographic trend is the relatively young populations of Pacific nations. As governments around the world prepare for ageing populations and growing demand for services and pensions, the Pacific remains comparatively youthful. That’s interestingly mirrored in the World Cup squads. In the women’s competition, New Zealand (median age 27 years) and Australia (26) have considerably older squads than Fiji and Samoa (both 22). The pattern is similar among the men, with New Zealand (29) and Australia (28) fielding older squads than Samoa (26) and Tonga (24). The differences are even more pronounced in the wider populations. The median ages of New Zealanders (37) and Australians (38) are much higher than those of people in Fiji (28), Tonga (21) and Samoa (20). Within New Zealand, we can point to a similar pattern. The median age of NZ Europeans is 42, compared with 29 for Fijian New Zealanders, 24 for Samoan New Zealanders and 22 for Tongan New Zealanders. These younger populations offer what we call a “demographic dividend”: the potential economic benefits as a growing share of the population enters its working and income-earning years. But these benefits aren’t automatic. Realising them requires investment in young people’s health, education and skills, as well as opportunities to develop their talents and aspirations. When talent meets opportunity Many players representing Pacific nations in this weekend’s semi-finals grew up a long way from the islands they now represent. They and their families were drawn to Australia and New Zealand by opportunities in education, employment and sport. Yet when the chance came, many chose to wear the jersey that reflects their identity, family ties and culture. Their achievements show what’s possible when young people have opportunities to develop their talents. Building on that momentum means continuing to invest in young people, on and off the field, so the next generation can thrive – wherever they call home. f2e22fb3444c9086: From Boo Jia Cher
The federal government’s plan to build 22km of covered pedestrian walkways across Kuala Lumpur is a welcome breath of fresh air.
For a city long dominated by cars, seeing Putrajaya and Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) invest RM55 million in walking infrastructure shows an encouraging shift in mindset.
It reflects the recognition of a basic truth: people won’t walk to buses and trains if they are soaked by sudden downpours or exhausted by intense heat, so they opt for the car instead.
A roof over our heads is a strong start, but it will not magically turn Kuala Lumpur into a walkable city overnight.
The theory of walkability

American urban designer Jeff Speck popularised the “General Theory of Walkability”, which states that for people to choose walking over driving, a path must meet four conditions at the same time: it must be useful, safe, comfortable, and interesting.
A covered walkway addresses only part of one of these conditions — making the walk more comfortable by blocking out rain and sun. On its own, shelter leaves the other three major gaps untouched:

Useful: A sheltered roof is useless if the path suddenly stops at a dead end, fails to connect to a train station, or nearby homes or shops. KL’s fragmented design often leaves transit stations, housing and shops all cut off from one another.

Safe: A roof cannot protect a pedestrian from a six-lane road with fast and dangerous traffic. If there are no safe crossings, traffic lights, or bollards separating people from speeding cars, walking will seem unsafe and people will still stay in their cars.

Interesting: Streets need active shopfronts, trees, and open views to feel secure and inviting. Just looking at how crowded certain parts of KL like Petaling Street or Jalan Tuanku Abdul Rahman get, even with their flaws, shows that with lots to see while walking, people will enjoy the walk.
If DBKL simply installs roofs over disconnected or dangerous paths, the RM55 million project risks becoming performative infrastructure; a ribbon-cutting gesture rather than a genuine transformation.
Get the right people involved
To get this right, the government needs more than just a construction budget; it needs an inclusive walkability commission.
This commission should carry out thorough, ground-level walking audits across every planned route. Crucially, these audits must be inclusive.

The team cannot just sit in offices looking at blueprints. They must walk the paths alongside wheelchair users, parents pushing strollers, senior citizens, visually impaired residents, and daily transit commuters, at different times of the day.
An inclusive audit asks practical, everyday questions:
Is the curb ramp too steep for a wheelchair user?
Does the covered walkway suddenly drop off into a high-speed slip road?
Are tactile paving tiles correctly aligned for visually impaired walkers?
Is there adequate street lighting to make the route safe at night?
More than roofs over walkways
Putting a roof over KL’s streets sends an important message: that walking matters.
But if we genuinely want people to leave their cars behind and use public transport, we need more than covered walkways. We need paths that are safe, continuous and accessible to everyone.
Even a covered walkway can feel uncomfortable when the surrounding streets are dark and deserted at night, with businesses shuttered.

A lack of activity after hours can make a place feel unsafe and discourage people from walking. This is part of a much bigger conversation about walkability, one that is inseparable from how we plan and build our cities.
Let’s not just cover our walkways. Let’s fix the walk, and the city around it.
Boo Jia Cher is an FMT reader.

cac1966d2368512b: A couple of billion for the thoughts of United’s Politburo at half-time in the Roma match on Tuesday.

United will get a look at how to build a club on Sunday when they visit Villa Park. A revamped young side will be gunning for them and the manager they wanted will be plotting their demise
Emery has found his perfect team and wants to build a dynasty there.
A 3-0 defeat at Barcelona was a reminder of how far they still need to travel.
But at least the new North Stand is taking shape, unlike the ‘ground under repair’ that is Old Trafford.
Progress all around. More than enough for Emery to turn down the poisoned chalice of United.

f87ca9d921a68dd3: Is China booming or stagnating? On one hand, its export industries—including electric vehicles, solar panels, and virtually the entire range of manufactured goods—are the envy of the world, and its tech and AI industries are second only to the US, with Europe trailing far behind.
On the other hand, as I have written many times, China is now in the sixth year of a full-blown, Japan-style real-estate crisis. Could China be booming and stagnating at the same time?

In a recent Brookings paper, the International Monetary Fund’s Yuanchen Yang and I explore the striking parallels between today’s China and Japan in the 1990s, especially in residential and commercial real estate as well as related infrastructure.
In both cases, the collapse of the speculative frenzy left a massive construction overhang that can take years to work off. China is still in the middle of that process.

Stunningly, China has built more square metres of residential property per capita than either the UK or France, despite still being a much poorer country. Its road and railway networks are on par with those of the world’s most advanced economies and, in many ways, far superior to America’s.
But the Chinese economy is also deeply unbalanced, like a bodybuilder who has bulked up only his torso. Consumption, the primary growth engine in advanced economies, remains weak.

Eastern China has marquee cities that are well on their way to rivaling their Western counterparts, yet in many smaller cities and rural areas, home to at least half of China’s population, living standards fall somewhere between those of Latin America and South Asia.

The fear now is that, with its housing bubble having collapsed, China may never escape the so-called middle-income trap. When Japan’s real-estate crisis hit, it was already a very wealthy country, with per-capita income rivaling that of the US.

Thirty years later, its per-capita income is closer to Italy’s, which in turn is below that of Mississippi, the poorest US state. And China today is nowhere near as rich as Japan was in the early 1990s.

Between automation and AI, the most dynamic parts of China’s most dynamic sectors are not creating enough jobs. Youth unemployment has gotten so bad that authorities no longer publish the figures regularly.

Even under the best of circumstances, it would be difficult to replace the sagging real-estate and infrastructure sector, which, as Yang and I show, accounts for nearly one-third of demand once both direct and indirect effects are included.

Still, it would be wrong to assume that China’s real-estate crisis necessarily constrains its ability to compete geopolitically or economically. If you speak to businesspeople or attend tech conferences, you will hear that China’s economy is dominant and innovative.
China is not a democracy, and its leaders can allow the dynamic tech and export sectors to flourish even as the rest of the domestic economy takes decades to work off the overbuilding binge.

It is entirely possible to imagine 450 million Chinese people flourishing in a dynamic economy dominated by tech and manufacturing, while the other 950 million get by at a much lower standard of living.
Faced with such a divide, most Western democracies would be overwhelmed by pressure for redistribution, as European countries already know well.

But that need not be the case in China, particularly if the government believes that national security and the country’s global role depend on bolstering its frontier sectors. And 450 million people is still more than the US population and on par with that of the European Union.
Whether such an outcome is possible, of course, remains to be seen. Since Xi Jinping became president in 2013, the Communist Party has paid considerable attention to regional disparities.
But the economic forces that concentrate activity in major hubs, together with the strong desire to assert power internationally, may ultimately trump the pressure to reduce inequality.

The great economic historian Angus Maddison, writing in the late 1960s, argued that—contrary to the views of many economists, including Paul Samuelson—the Soviet Union would never fully catch up with the US. Nevertheless, thanks to its rich scientific tradition, the USSR could still compete at the technological frontier and achieve military parity.
One major difference between the Soviet Union and China is that China has bent over backwards to integrate with the US, both in trade and in science.
Despite US president Donald Trump’s trade war, it is clear that today’s challenges, from climate change to rogue AI, cannot be solved without extensive cooperation between the two superpowers.

So, as paralysing as China’s real-estate crisis has been, and even though excess construction will likely hold down growth for years to come, the dynamic core of its economy will keep thriving, so long as the country remains politically stable—and does not succumb to the temptations of imperial overreach.

Kenneth Rogoff, a former chief economist of the International Monetary Fund, is professor of economics and public policy at Harvard University and the recipient of the 2011 Deutsche Bank Prize in Financial Economics.

If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training

c61645b48e45a038: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Archaeologists have discovered the oldest direct evidence of psychoactive cannabis use in a Siberian tomb that dates back 2,800 years and was the site of human and horse sacrifices, according to a study published on Thursday in Science.

During excavations of the tomb, a team found more than 1,400 cannabis seeds scattered around the remains of several Iron Age individuals, and even identified cannabinoids—including the active compound tetrahydrocannabinol (THC)—in a person’s preserved hair.

Though humans cultivated cannabis for many millennia before the Iron Age, this is by far the earliest clear-cut proof that the plant was consumed for its psychoactive effects, which have made it one of the most widely used drugs in the world today.

The discovery is “absolutely crazy,” said Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology and the University of Bern who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. “People have been speculating a lot about psychoactive use of cannabis in the past, but to actually pin it down and prove it with soft tissue evidence of the humans involved—that is something very special.
“That is an absolutely unique and extremely rare combination of evidence,” he added.

Cannabis has a multifaceted history as a recreational drug and a pop cultural touchstone, as well as a traditional medicine that has been used for millennia by many cultures, including in China, Russia, and around the Mediterranean Basin. Humans began cultivating the plant as early as 10,000 years ago for its oil and fiber, but the origins of its specific consumption as a psychoactive substance is unclear.

Cannabis was important to the Scythian culture, a horse-riding people that emerged on the Eurasian steppes in the 9th century BCE and became a major force in the subsequent centuries. The historian Herodotus described Scythian rituals that involved ceremonial burning of cannabis in enclosed spaces, and their cannabis residues and products have been found at Scythian archaeological sites.

“Herodotus speaks about the Scythians being quite fond of cannabis in the first place, so this has always been in the back of our minds,” Caspari said. “But it is so incredibly rare to find well-preserved plant remains that this is not really something you can hope for or look for. This is ultimately complete luck and chance.”

Now, Caspari and his colleagues have hit an archaeological jackpot at a tomb known as Tunnug 1, located in Siberia’s Uyuk River Valley. Six elite individuals are interred in the interior of the royal mound inside several tree-trunk coffins and wooden structures. They are mostly men, though one woman is also present. The mound is lined with remains of sacrificed humans, as well as dozens of sacrificed horses, close to the surface.

As the team carefully worked through the layers of the burial, they found hundreds of cannabis seeds distributed around the bodies that were dated to the 8th century BCE. However, the real smoking blunt was the detection of cannabinols in preserved hair samples, including traces of THC, the most important mind-altering compound in cannabis.

The results confirm contemporaneous accounts of Scythians as cannabis consumers who used the plant for purification and mortuary rituals. It’s possible that the people selected as human sacrifice consumed the drug to prepare them for their unenviable fate.

“It being in a burial context, of course, there's a ritual aspect to it,” Caspari explained. “It might be a little bit more sinister, but this is speculation. We do have a lot of horse sacrifices and also some human sacrifices on the surface of the mound. And if you imagine humans being sacrificed, they usually don't like that very much. It might be advantageous to have them dosed a little bit, at least, to make the procedure a bit more humane, if you will.”
“Of course, that is speculation,” he cautioned. “We don't have any written sources about that particular area, but that's at least one way we could go with our interpretation.”

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The researchers hope to learn more about the context and meaning of the cannabis use at Tunnug 1 through continued excavations and an analysis of more hair samples. What’s more, the team plans to conduct DNA analysis on the seeds, an approach that could yield new insights about the murky history of cannabis domestication and its early use as a psychoactive substance. This line of research could also shed light on modern cannabis strains, and may even be revived for new medicinal or recreational purposes.

“We've already sequenced part of the seeds to unravel and disentangle the domestication history,” Caspari said. “Funnily enough, we don't even know what wild cannabis actually looks like because there has been so much intermixing and interbreeding since the 70s, when people started experimenting and trying to get more potent drug variants. Some of the initial landraces and the actual wild cannabis has been lost.”

“Now, having DNA that's almost 3,000 years old, we will be able to take that step back into the past and see what an unaltered cannabis would have looked like,” he said. “In the ideal case, we might even be able to work together with the medical industry and bring some of these very ancient genetics back into cannabis production to potentially help people with very interesting and distinctive cannabinoid combinations.”

Put that in your pipe and smoke it. Regardless of where future research into this ancient plant leads, this long-sought evidence of cannabis use thousands of years ago confirms the rich cultural legacy of the plant across time and space.

“As an archeologist, I might be a bit biased here, but I think the history and cultural practices really do matter,” Caspari concluded. “I think our findings do indeed inform current discussions on legalization, on usage of medical cannabis—which is very much an ongoing discourse—and I think what we've been able to do with this study is provide an anchor, and show that there is this deep cultural history to the use of cannabis as a psychoactive drug.”
